11.overview: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati, head of the Edneer Mutt in Kasaragod, challenged Kerala land reform legislation under Article 32. While the petition was pending, Parliament enacted the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments to bypass the ruling in Golak Nath and insulate Ninth Schedule laws from judicial review. A historic 13-judge Constitution Bench was assembled to decide whether Parliament's amending power under Article 368 was absolute or subject to inherent constitutional limitations.
11.issues: Whether Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is unlimited, and whether constitutional amendments can abrogate or emasculate fundamental rights under Part III.
11.holding: By a 7:6 majority, the Supreme Court established the Basic Structure Doctrine. Parliament holds plenary power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot alter, damage, or destroy the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.
key_findings: The power to amend under Article 368 is a constituent power, not ordinary legislative power, but the word 'amend' implies that the original constitutional identity cannot be destroyed.
Parliament cannot rewrite or replace the Constitution with an entirely new document or abrogate its fundamental democratic framework.
Core features including supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic governance, separation of powers, and secularism form the inviolable basic structure.
Judicial review is an indispensable constitutional mechanism to enforce the basic structure limitation against unconstitutional amendments.
Article 13(2) does not apply to constitutional amendments under Article 368, thereby overruling the contrary holding in Golak Nath.
Section 4 of the 25th Amendment Act, which barred judicial review of laws declared to further Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and (c), was held unconstitutional.
The basic structure doctrine harmonizes popular parliamentary sovereignty with constitutional supremacy and protection of human rights.

provisions.title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to establish that the power of constitutional amendment is subject to the implied limitation of the Basic Structure Doctrine.

provisions.title: Laws inconsistent with fundamental rights
provisions.relevance: Examined regarding whether 'law' in Article 13(2) includes constitutional amendments; Golak Nath overruled on this point.

provisions.title: Remedies for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as a foundational pillar of the basic structure enabling citizens to challenge unconstitutional amendments.

provisions.title: Saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles
provisions.relevance: First part upheld, but the conclusive declaration clause barring judicial review was severed and struck down.

12.overview: A retired High Court judge, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy, challenged the constitutional validity of the Union Government's biometric identification project (Aadhaar). When the State contended that early decisions in M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) precluded any fundamental right to privacy, the matter was referred to a 9-judge Constitution Bench to conclusively resolve the constitutional status of privacy.
12.issues: Whether the Right to Privacy is guaranteed as an independent Fundamental Right under the Constitution of India, and whether the earlier decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh laid down correct law.
12.holding: A unanimous 9-judge Constitution Bench held that privacy is a fundamental, natural, and inalienable right protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed by Part III.
key_findings: Privacy is not a granted privilege but an inalienable natural right inherent to human dignity, autonomy, and bodily integrity.
M.P. Sharma was overruled to the extent it held privacy is not a fundamental right, and the majority observations in Kharak Singh were formally overruled.
Privacy encompasses three critical facets: bodily privacy, spatial privacy, and informational privacy / personal data autonomy.
Any state encroachment on privacy must satisfy a rigorous three-fold test: legality (existence of law), legitimate state aim, and proportionality.
Informational privacy requires that individuals have control over the collection, storage, and processing of their personal data by state and non-state entities.
The right extends protection against state surveillance, unauthorized profiling, and psychological intrusion.
Sexual orientation and intimate personal choices are protected facets of privacy and constitutional liberty under Article 21.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Recognized as the primary constitutional repository of the right to privacy, encompassing personal autonomy and dignity.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Invoked to subject arbitrary privacy intrusions to non-arbitrariness review.

provisions.title: Protection of freedoms
provisions.relevance: Protects informational privacy, free expression, movement, and private association from unjustified state surveillance.

13.overview: The Regional Passport Officer, New Delhi, impounded the passport of journalist Maneka Gandhi under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 'in the public interest' without furnishing reasons or providing a pre-decisional hearing. The petitioner approached the Supreme Court under Article 32 challenging the administrative order as arbitrary and violative of her fundamental rights to personal liberty, free speech, and freedom of movement.
13.issues: Whether the right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21, and whether 'procedure established by law' requires that such procedure must be just, fair, and reasonable conforming to natural justice.
13.holding: The 7-judge Constitution Bench held that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, oppressive, or fanciful; it must be just, fair, and reasonable. The Golden Triangle doctrine established that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are mutually reinforcing and not water-tight compartments.
key_findings: The right to travel abroad is an integral component of 'personal liberty' protected under Article 21.

Procedure established by law under Article 21 must satisfy the standards of fairness, reasonableness, and justice, effectively incorporating substantive due process principles into Indian jurisprudence.

Articles 14, 19, and 21 form a constitutional trinity or 'Golden Triangle'; a law depriving personal liberty must simultaneously pass the tests of non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and reasonableness under Article 19.
Principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem) are implicit in Article 21 and must be read into statutory provisions unless excluded by clear legislative necessity.
Post-decisional hearing was accepted in this case as curing the initial absence of notice, avoiding mechanical invalidation of administrative steps taken for urgent reasons.
The narrow literal interpretation of Article 21 adopted in A.K. Gopalan was conclusively buried.
Executive discretion to curtail fundamental freedoms without communicating reasons is antithetical to the rule of law.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Transformed from a literal procedural check into a substantive guarantee requiring just, fair, and reasonable procedure.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied as an overarching test against arbitrary administrative action affecting personal liberty.

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression
provisions.relevance: Held to be affected when the right to travel abroad for journalistic activities was curtailed.

provisions.title: Impounding of passport in the public interest
provisions.relevance: Statutory power subjected to mandatory natural justice requirements and reasonable justification.

14.overview: LGBTQ+ activists, dancers, and professionals challenged the constitutional validity of Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalized 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature'. The petitioners argued that criminalizing consensual sexual acts between adults in private violated the rights to equality, non-discrimination, freedom of expression, and bodily privacy.
14.issues: Whether Section 377 IPC, to the extent that it criminalizes consensual sexual conduct between adults in private, violates Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
14.holding: A unanimous 5-judge Constitution Bench read down Section 377 IPC, holding that consensual sexual acts between consenting adults in private are decriminalized. The Court overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2014) and affirmed full constitutional equality for LGBTQ+ citizens.
key_findings: Constitutional morality must triumph over majoritarian or social morality in adjudicating fundamental rights.
Sexual orientation is an innate, biological attribute and an integral facet of individual identity, privacy, and personal autonomy.
Discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited under Article 15(1) as a form of sex-based discrimination.
Section 377's application to consenting adults is manifestly arbitrary under Article 14, lacking any rational nexus with a legitimate state purpose.
Bodily autonomy and freedom to choose an intimate partner are protected liberties under Article 21 and Article 19(1)(a).
The ruling in Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation was formally overruled as flawed and regressive.
Section 377 remains valid only regarding non-consensual sexual acts, bestiality, and sexual offenses against minors.

provisions.title: Unnatural offences
provisions.relevance: Read down so that private consensual sexual activity between consenting adults is no longer a criminal offence.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied via the doctrine of manifest arbitrariness to strike down the criminalization of consensual acts.

provisions.title: Prohibition of discrimination
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to include discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation within the ambit of 'sex'.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as guaranteeing personal autonomy, dignity, and intimate relational privacy.

15.overview: The Executive Chairman of the Legal Aid Services West Bengal addressed a letter to the Chief Justice regarding custodial deaths in police lockups. Treating the communication as a PIL under Article 32, the Court examined widespread custodial violence and torture by law enforcement agencies and addressed the urgent need for structural safeguards during arrest and interrogation.
15.issues: What preventive, punitive, and remedial measures are required to eradicate custodial violence, torture, and deaths in police custody while safeguarding human rights under Articles 21 and 22.
15.holding: The Supreme Court formulated 11 mandatory, binding guidelines to govern every arrest and detention in India. The Court held that custodial torture violates human dignity under Article 21 and affirmed monetary compensation for constitutional torts.
key_findings: Custodial violence, torture, and lockup deaths constitute serious infringements of the rule of law and human dignity under Article 21.
Police personnel carrying out arrest and interrogation must bear accurate, visible, and clear identification and name tags.
An arrest memo specifying date, time, and signed by at least one respectable witness must be prepared at the time of arrest.
The arrested person has the right to have a friend, relative, or person interested in their welfare informed of their arrest within 8 to 12 hours.
The arrested person must be medically examined at the time of arrest and re-examined every 48 hours by a trained medical officer.
Copies of all arrest documents and memos must be forwarded to the local Magistrate for judicial oversight.
Failure by police officers to adhere to the guidelines renders them liable for departmental disciplinary action as well as contempt of court.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Formulated the bedrock for holding custodial violence strictly prohibited even against criminal suspects.

provisions.title: Protection against arrest and detention
provisions.relevance: Enforced procedural safeguards including the right to know grounds of arrest and consult legal counsel.

provisions.title: Procedure of arrest and duties of officer
provisions.relevance: Later codified into CrPC pursuant to the guidelines laid down in this landmark verdict.

provisions.title: Obligation to inform relative of arrest
provisions.relevance: Legislatively enacted into the procedural code directly reflecting the D.K. Basu arrest notification mandate.

16.overview: A minor girl was kidnapped, and despite repeated approaches to the police station, the police officer refused to register an FIR and delayed action for days. A writ petition was filed under Article 32 to determine whether police officers have discretion to conduct a preliminary inquiry before registering an FIR when information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence.
16.issues: Whether registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure upon receipt of information disclosing a cognizable offence, or whether the police officer has the discretion to conduct a preliminary inquiry first.
16.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC if information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. Police officers possess no discretion to conduct a preliminary inquiry in such situations.
key_findings: The use of the word 'shall' in Section 154(1) CrPC indicates mandatory legislative intent; registration cannot be delayed or avoided.
The police officer cannot evaluate whether the information is credible or reasonable prior to registering the FIR.
Preliminary inquiry is permissible only in exceptional categories: matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence cases, corruption cases, or abnormal delay cases.
Where preliminary inquiry is permissible, it must be limited to verifying whether the information discloses a cognizable offence and not to ascertain truth.
A preliminary inquiry must be concluded expeditiously within a maximum period of 7 days (later clarified up to 15 days in exceptional circumstances).
Delinquent police officers who refuse to register an FIR disclose disciplinary delinquency and face statutory prosecution under Section 166A IPC.
Mandatory FIR registration safeguards complainant rights, ensures prompt collection of evidence, and curtails police manipulation.

provisions.title: Information in cognizable cases (FIR)
provisions.relevance: Interpreted as strictly mandatory, obligating station house officers to register an FIR without subjective discretion.

provisions.title: Public servant disobeying direction under law
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as the penal consequence for law enforcement officers refusing to register mandatory FIRs.

provisions.title: Information in cognizable cases
provisions.relevance: Corresponds to Section 154 CrPC in the new procedural framework, adopting the Lalita Kumari mandatory mandate.

17.overview: The appellant, Arnesh Kumar, faced arrest under Section 498A IPC (cruelty by husband or relatives) and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act following matrimonial disputes. He approached the Supreme Court seeking anticipatory bail, prompting the Court to examine the rampant problem of mechanical, indiscriminate arrests under Section 498A and other offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years.
17.issues: Whether police officers can mechanically arrest accused persons under Section 498A IPC without satisfying the objective necessity criteria specified in Section 41 CrPC, and what remedies exist against arbitrary detention.
17.holding: The Supreme Court issued mandatory directions prohibiting mechanical arrests in offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years. Police officers must satisfy the preconditions under Section 41(1)(b) CrPC and issue a notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC before effecting arrest.
key_findings: Arrest brings humiliation, curtails freedom, and casts scars forever; power to arrest must be distinguished from the necessity to arrest.
In offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years, arrest cannot be made merely because a cognizable case is registered.
Police officers must be provided with a checklist containing the specific grounds specified under Section 41(1)(b)(ii) CrPC.
The arresting officer must record written reasons justifying why arrest is necessary (to prevent further offences, prevent tampering, or secure attendance).
Magistrates cannot authorize mechanical remand under Section 167 CrPC without perusing the police checklist and independent satisfaction.
Failure to comply with Section 41/41A CrPC renders the arresting officer liable for departmental proceedings and contempt of court.
Judicial Magistrates authorizing detention without recording satisfaction are subject to disciplinary action by the High Court.

provisions.title: When police may arrest without warrant
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to require mandatory objective justification and recorded reasons before arresting without warrant.

provisions.title: Notice of appearance before police officer
provisions.relevance: Established as the default procedural requirement instead of custodial arrest for offences up to 7 years.

provisions.title: Husband or relative of husband subjecting woman to cruelty
provisions.relevance: Subjected to strict procedural oversight to prevent mechanical harassment and misuse of penal machinery.

provisions.title: When police may arrest without warrant
provisions.relevance: The corresponding BNSS provision codifying the safeguards against mechanical arrest.

18.overview: The appellant was convicted of murdering three family members and sentenced to death under Section 302 IPC. The Supreme Court heard a constitutional challenge to the validity of the death penalty under Section 302 IPC and Section 354(3) CrPC on the grounds that capital punishment violates Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
18.issues: Whether the death penalty provided under Section 302 IPC and Section 354(3) CrPC is unconstitutional, and what principles govern judicial discretion in awarding capital punishment.
18.holding: A 4:1 majority of the 5-judge Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of capital punishment under Section 302 IPC and Section 354(3) CrPC, propounding the landmark 'Rarest of Rare Cases' doctrine.
key_findings: The death penalty for murder does not violate Article 19 or 21, as the Constitution itself contemplates deprivation of life by 'procedure established by law'.
Under Section 354(3) CrPC, life imprisonment is the general rule and the death sentence is the exceptional sentence requiring special reasons.
Capital punishment must be restricted only to the 'rarest of rare cases' where the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
Sentencing courts must carry out a comprehensive balancing test weighing aggravating circumstances against mitigating circumstances.
The mitigating circumstances of the offender—including age, mental condition, possibility of reformation, and socioeconomic background—must be given full weight.
A real and abiding concern for the dignity of human life postulates that death should not be awarded unless the crime is so abhorrent that society's conscience demands it.
Justice P.N. Bhagwati delivered a celebrated lone dissent arguing that capital punishment is cruel, arbitrary, and violative of Articles 14 and 21.

provisions.title: Punishment for murder
provisions.relevance: Constitutional validity of capital punishment as an alternative punishment was upheld by the majority.

provisions.title: Special reasons for death penalty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to establish that life imprisonment is the rule and capital sentence the rare exception requiring recorded special reasons.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Held not violated by capital punishment when awarded through just, fair, and non-arbitrary judicial procedure.

19.overview: Shayara Bano, a Muslim woman who was abruptly divorced through instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) via a speed post letter, filed a writ petition under Article 32 challenging the practice along with nikah halala and polygamy. A 5-judge Constitution Bench comprising judges of five different religious backgrounds was constituted to determine the constitutional validity of talaq-e-biddat.
19.issues: Whether the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instant triple talaq) is protected as an essential religious practice under Article 25 of the Constitution, or whether it violates fundamental rights under Article 14.
19.holding: By a 3:2 majority, the Supreme Court declared the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instant triple talaq) to be unconstitutional, arbitrary, and void in law. The Court held that what is bad in theology cannot be good in law.
key_findings: Talaq-e-biddat is not an essential religious practice of Islam, as it is considered sinful and disapproved by Islamic jurists themselves.
Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 recognized talaq, subjecting it to constitutional review under Article 13(1).
Instant triple talaq permits a Muslim man to sever the marital tie whimsically and capriciously without any attempt at reconciliation, violating Article 14.
The doctrine of 'manifest arbitrariness' was firmly established as an independent ground under Article 14 to invalidate both statutory provisions and state-recognized customs.
Legislation or custom that is capricious, irrational, or without adequate determining principle is manifestly arbitrary.
Fundamental rights under Part III prevail over discriminatory personal law practices that are not protected as core religious tenets.
Chief Justice Khehar and Justice Abdul Nazeer dissented, holding that personal law is outside Part III and recommended legislative intervention.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied through the doctrine of manifest arbitrariness to strike down the unilateral practice of instant triple talaq.

provisions.title: Freedom of conscience and free profession of religion
provisions.relevance: Held not to protect talaq-e-biddat because it was not an essential religious practice of Islam.

provisions.title: Section 2
provisions.relevance: Held to bring rules regarding marriage and divorce within the definition of 'laws in force' subject to constitutional review.

20.overview: An Indian expatriate, Joseph Shine, challenged the constitutional validity of Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 198(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 497 criminalized adultery but punished only the male paramour, treated the woman as a victim devoid of agency, and excused the act if committed with the consent or connivance of the woman's husband.
20.issues: Whether Section 497 IPC and Section 198(2) CrPC violate Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution by discriminating on the basis of sex and denying women constitutional agency, equality, and dignity.
20.holding: A unanimous 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down Section 497 of the IPC and Section 198(2) of the CrPC as unconstitutional, holding that adultery can be a ground for civil divorce but cannot remain a criminal offence.
key_findings: Section 497 IPC treated a married woman as the chattel or property of her husband, violating her fundamental right to human dignity under Article 21.
The exemption granted when adultery occurred with the husband's 'consent or connivance' reduced the woman to a possession whose violation depended on the master's assent.
The provision discriminated on grounds of sex under Article 15(1) by denying women the right to prosecute an unfaithful husband or the female paramour.
Section 497 was manifestly arbitrary under Article 14 because it punished only the man while assuming the woman was incapable of independent moral agency.
Criminalizing marital infidelity represents an unwarranted state intrusion into the private, intimate domain of individuals.
Adultery remains a valid ground for civil remedies including divorce and dissolution of marriage, but state penal coercion is illegitimate.
The earlier decisions in Sowmithri Vishnu (1985) and V. Revathi (1988) upholding the provision were overruled.

provisions.title: Adultery
provisions.relevance: Struck down in its entirety as unconstitutional and violative of Articles 14, 15, and 21.

provisions.title: Prosecution for offences against marriage
provisions.relevance: Declared unconstitutional to the extent it permitted only the husband to file a complaint of adultery.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied to condemn the unequal and arbitrary patriarchal classifications underpinning the penal provision.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as protecting female agency, dignity, and private intimate autonomy.

21.overview: In an election petition challenging the election of an MLA to the Kerala Legislative Assembly, the petitioner sought to introduce electronic records (CDs, audio files, and video recordings of political speeches) without obtaining a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act. The dispute raised the critical question of whether electronic records could be admitted as secondary evidence without complying with special statutory certificate requirements.
21.issues: Whether electronic records can be admitted as secondary evidence under Sections 63 and 65 of the Indian Evidence Act without fulfilling the mandatory certificate requirement prescribed under Section 65B(4).
21.holding: A 3-judge Bench held that Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act constitutes a complete and special code for the admissibility of electronic records. Secondary evidence of electronic records is inadmissible unless accompanied by a mandatory Section 65B(4) certificate.
key_findings: Electronic records are susceptible to tampering, alteration, and erasure; strict procedural safeguards under Section 65B are essential to ensure evidentiary integrity.
Section 65B is a special provision that completely overrides the general provisions relating to secondary evidence in Sections 63 and 65 (generalia specialibus non derogant).
If an electronic record is produced from primary custody by the author/owner who produced it directly, Section 65B(4) certificate is not required.
However, if electronic evidence is sought to be produced as secondary evidence, a certificate under Section 65B(4) is an indispensable condition precedent to admissibility.
The earlier contrary view in State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu (Parliament Attack Case) holding that secondary evidence could be produced under Section 65 without a 65B certificate was overruled.
The certificate must identify the electronic record, describe the manner of its creation, and be signed by a responsible official in charge of the device.
Oral evidence cannot substitute for the mandatory Section 65B certificate.

provisions.title: Admissibility of electronic records
provisions.relevance: Interpreted as a special mandatory code overriding Sections 63 and 65 for electronic secondary evidence.

provisions.title: Secondary evidence
provisions.relevance: Held inapplicable to electronic records unless filtered through Section 65B.

provisions.title: Admissibility of electronic records
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision in the new BSA retaining the mandatory certificate framework.

22.overview: In an election dispute concerning an assembly constituency in Maharashtra, video recordings of nomination proceedings were sought to be produced from Election Commission computers, but the authorities delayed or failed to issue the certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act. A reference was made to a 3-judge Bench to resolve conflicting decisions in Anvar P.V. and Shafhi Mohammad regarding the timing and mandatory nature of the Section 65B certificate.
22.issues: Whether the certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act is mandatory even when a party is unable to procure it from a hostile third party, and at what stage of the criminal or civil trial must the certificate be produced.
22.holding: A 3-judge Bench authoritatively settled the law: the Section 65B(4) certificate is mandatory for secondary electronic evidence, but the court has wide powers under Section 311 CrPC and Section 165 Evidence Act to summon the certificate at any stage before the trial concludes.
key_findings: Section 65B(4) certificate is an absolute requirement for admitting secondary evidence of an electronic record.
The certificate is not required if the original electronic device itself is produced directly in court (primary evidence).
The decision in Shafhi Mohammad v. State of H.P., which held that a certificate can be dispensed with if an accused/party lacks access to the device, was overruled as bad law.
A party unable to obtain a certificate from a person in control of the device can apply to the Court to issue a summons under Section 91/311 CrPC or Section 165 Evidence Act to compel production.
The certificate need not necessarily accompany the chargesheet or initial pleading; it can be produced at any stage of trial prior to the closing of evidence.
In criminal trials, the accused must be given a fair opportunity to inspect the electronic record and cross-examine the certificate issuer.
Telecom service providers and mobile network operators must preserve call detail records (CDRs) and server logs for an adequate duration under licensing guidelines.

provisions.title: Certificate for electronic evidence
provisions.relevance: Mandatory nature reaffirmed while prescribing remedial procedures to summon missing certificates.

provisions.title: Power to summon material witness or examine person present
provisions.relevance: Applied as an enabling power to direct production of electronic certificates during trial.

provisions.title: Admissibility of electronic records and certificate
provisions.relevance: The updated statutory equivalent under the new evidence enactment.

23.overview: A special leave petition arose out of non-compliance with statutory arrest and bail provisions by investigating agencies and trial courts across India. The Supreme Court observed that undertrial prisoners crowded Indian jails (over 70% of prison populations), largely due to mechanical arrests and unnecessary insistence on surety bonds, prompting the Court to issue comprehensive nationwide guidelines on bail jurisprudence.
23.issues: What guidelines should govern investigating agencies and trial courts to prevent unjustified pre-trial detention, streamline bail adjudication, and enforce Sections 41, 41A, 88, 170, and 436A of the CrPC.
23.holding: The Supreme Court issued comprehensive, binding guidelines categorizing criminal offences into four distinct categories (A, B, C, D) and directed trial courts to decide bail applications expeditiously without insisting on custodial detention when accused cooperate with investigation.
key_findings: Bail is the rule and jail is the exception; personal liberty under Article 21 cannot be compromised by mechanical pre-trial incarceration.
Category A offences (punishable up to 7 years without minimum sentence): bail should ordinarily be granted on appearance without police remand if accused cooperated under Section 41A.
Category B offences (heinous offences punishable with death, life, or over 7 years): bail applications to be decided on merits with reasoned orders.
Category C offences (special acts like NDPS, PMLA, UAPA, POCSO): bail to be decided on merits subject to statutory reverse-burden conditions.
Category D offences (economic offences not covered by special acts): bail to be evaluated considering nature of economic loss and role played.
Section 436A CrPC mandates release of undertrial prisoners who have completed half of the maximum prescribed period of imprisonment.
The Union of India was urged to consider enacting a standalone 'Bail Act' along the lines of the United Kingdom Bail Act to streamline bail administration.

provisions.title: Notice of appearance before police officer
provisions.relevance: Non-compliance held to entitle the accused to immediate bail without police remand.

provisions.title: Maximum period for which an undertrial prisoner can be detained
provisions.relevance: Mandatorily enforced to release prisoners languishing beyond half the maximum statutory sentence.

provisions.title: Power to take bond for appearance
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to require courts to accept personal bonds rather than remanding cooperative accused.

provisions.title: Maximum period of detention for undertrials
provisions.relevance: The updated procedural provision providing relief for first-time offenders and long-term undertrials.

24.overview: The Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR), the Communist Party of India (Marxist), and other petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Electoral Bond Scheme, 2018 introduced by the Union Government via the Finance Act, 2017. The scheme permitted anonymous corporate and individual donations to registered political parties via interest-free bearer banking instruments.
24.issues: Whether the Electoral Bond Scheme and consequential amendments to the Reserve Bank of India Act, Representation of the People Act, Companies Act, and Income Tax Act violate the voters' fundamental right to information under Article 19(1)(a).
24.holding: A unanimous 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme and amendments to Section 31(3) of the RBI Act, Section 29C of the RP Act, Section 182 of the Companies Act, and Section 13A of the IT Act as unconstitutional and manifestly arbitrary.
key_findings: The voter's right to information about political funding and candidates is an integral part of the fundamental freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
Anonymity in political contributions deprives voters of vital knowledge regarding potential quid pro quo arrangements between corporate donors and political parties.
The curb on black money, while a legitimate state objective, failed the constitutional proportionality test because less intrusive alternatives existed.

The amendment to Section 182 of the Companies Act, which removed the 7.5% net profit cap and permitted loss-making and shell companies to donate unlimited amounts, was manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.
The State Bank of India (SBI) was directed to stop issuing electoral bonds immediately and furnish complete purchase and redemption data to the Election Commission of India.
The Election Commission of India was directed to publish all donor and recipient details on its official website for public inspection.
Corporate contributions cannot be equated with individual political expression; unlimited corporate funding distorts democratic electoral parity.

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression (Right to Information)
provisions.relevance: Held violated by anonymous electoral bonds because informed voting is essential to participatory democracy.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied through manifest arbitrariness to strike down unlimited corporate funding without profit limits.

provisions.title: Declaration of donation by a political party
provisions.relevance: The exemption granted to electoral bonds from statutory disclosure was struck down as unconstitutional.

provisions.title: Prohibitions and restrictions regarding political contributions
provisions.relevance: Amendment removing the 7.5% profit cap on corporate political donations was declared unconstitutional.

25.overview: Bhanwari Devi, a Dalit social worker in Rajasthan, was gang-raped by dominant-caste men in retaliation for stopping a child marriage. When the criminal trial faced systemic indifference, social activist groups and NGOs filed a PIL under Article 32 highlighting the pervasive menace of sexual harassment of working women and the absolute vacuum in Indian statutory law to protect women in workplaces.
25.issues: Whether gender equality and personal liberty under Articles 14, 19, and 21 guarantee women freedom from sexual harassment at the workplace, and whether the Supreme Court can formulate binding guidelines in the absence of legislation.
25.holding: A 3-judge Bench held that sexual harassment at the workplace violates Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g), and 21 of the Constitution. In the absence of legislative enactment, the Court formulated the binding 'Vishaka Guidelines' to operate as law under Article 141.
key_findings: Gender equality encompasses protection from sexual harassment and the right to work with dignity, which is a universally recognized basic human right.
In the absence of domestic legislation, international conventions and norms like the CEDAW Convention can be read into fundamental rights to enlarge their scope.
Every incident of sexual harassment violates the fundamental rights of gender equality (Article 14), non-discrimination (Article 15), and the right to life and liberty (Article 21).
The right to practice any profession or carry on any trade or occupation under Article 19(1)(g) includes the right to a safe workplace environment.
Employers and responsible authorities in public and private workplaces have a mandatory duty to prevent and deter sexual harassment.
The Court mandated the creation of an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) with a woman presiding officer and NGO participation to resolve complaints.
The Vishaka Guidelines operated as binding statutory law across India until Parliament enacted the POSH Act, 2013.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Anchored the principle of gender equality prohibiting sexist harassment in employment.

provisions.title: Right to practice any profession, trade or business
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to guarantee a safe, non-hostile working environment for women employees.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Guarantees the fundamental human right to work with dignity without humiliation or assault.

provisions.title: Law declared by Supreme Court to be binding
provisions.relevance: Invoked to give the Vishaka Guidelines the force of binding statutory law across India pending parliamentary enactment.

26.overview: Communist leader A.K. Gopalan was detained in Madras Central Jail under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950. He challenged the detention order under Article 32, arguing that Section 14 of the Act and his preventive detention violated his fundamental freedoms under Articles 19 and 21, and that 'procedure established by law' must be construed as equivalent to the American 'due process of law'.
26.issues: Whether 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 means natural justice or due process of law, and whether Articles 19 and 21 operate conjunctively or as mutually exclusive provisions.
26.holding: A 6-judge Constitution Bench held that 'procedure established by law' meant procedure enacted by a competent legislature (lex), rejecting substantive due process. The Court held that Articles 19 and 21 are mutually exclusive compartments (later overruled in Maneka Gandhi).
key_findings: The phrase 'procedure established by law' was deliberately adopted by the constituent assembly instead of 'due process of law' to avoid judicial veto over social policy.
Under Article 21, 'law' means state-made enacted law and does not incorporate principles of natural justice.
Article 19 applies only to free citizens and cannot be invoked by a person lawfully deprived of personal liberty under Article 21 or 22.
Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, which prohibited the detainee from disclosing the grounds of detention to a court of law, was held unconstitutional and severed.
Preventive detention is a constitutional necessity recognized under Article 22, provided procedural safeguards under Article 22(5) are satisfied.
Justice Fazl Ali delivered a historic dissenting opinion, arguing that fundamental rights form a coherent whole and procedure must conform to natural justice.
The majority doctrine of water-tight compartments was eventually repudiated in R.C. Cooper (1970) and Maneka Gandhi (1978).

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Literally interpreted as requiring only formal legislative procedure, distinguishing it from substantive due process.

provisions.title: Protection against arrest and preventive detention
provisions.relevance: Applied as a self-contained code for preventive detention.

provisions.title: Bar on disclosing grounds of detention
provisions.relevance: Struck down as an unconstitutional bar on judicial review.

27.overview: The State of Madras issued a 'Communal G.O.' allocating fixed quotas of seats in state medical and engineering colleges based strictly on religion, caste, and community. Smt. Champakam Dorairajan, a Brahmin candidate, was denied admission despite securing higher marks than admitted candidates of other quotas, leading to a challenge under Article 32.
27.issues: Whether the Communal G.O. violated Article 29(2) of the Constitution, and whether Directive Principles of State Policy under Article 46 can override Fundamental Rights under Part III.
27.holding: A 7-judge Constitution Bench held that the Communal G.O. violated Article 29(2) by denying admission solely on grounds of religion and caste. The Court established that Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and prevail over Directive Principles in the event of conflict.
key_findings: Article 29(2) explicitly prohibits denial of admission into state-funded educational institutions on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or language.
The Communal G.O. made caste and community the sole basis for seat distribution, rendering it unconstitutional.
Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are non-justiciable and cannot override or abridge the justiciable Fundamental Rights in Part III.
Directive Principles must run subsidiary to Fundamental Rights, though the State must strive to implement them harmoniously.
The historic judgment led directly to Parliament enacting the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, which inserted Article 15(4).
Article 15(4) was specifically introduced to enable the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes.
Established the baseline equality jurisprudence for educational admissions in independent India.

provisions.title: Protection of interests of minorities - Non-discrimination in admissions
provisions.relevance: Directly applied to invalidate caste-based reservation quotas in medical college admissions.

provisions.title: Promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections
provisions.relevance: Held to be subservient to the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III.

provisions.title: Special provision for advancement of backward classes
provisions.relevance: Direct constitutional consequence: inserted by 1st Amendment, 1951 to overcome this judgment.

28.overview: Following the enactment of the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951—which introduced Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule to insulate land reform legislation from challenges under fundamental rights—zamindars and landholders, led by Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo, challenged the amendment's constitutional validity under Article 32.
28.issues: Whether the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 was invalid because it abridged fundamental property rights under Part III, and whether 'law' in Article 13(2) includes a constitutional amendment made under Article 368.
28.holding: A unanimous 5-judge Constitution Bench upheld the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951. The Court held that constituent power under Article 368 is distinct from ordinary legislative power and that a constitutional amendment does not constitute 'law' under Article 13(2).
key_findings: The terms of Article 368 are plenary and empower Parliament to amend any provision of the Constitution without exception.
The word 'law' in Article 13(2) must be read as referring to rules, regulations, or ordinary statutory enactments made in exercise of legislative power, not constitutional amendments.
Constituent power exercised under Article 368 is sovereign and distinct from ordinary statutory law-making power under Articles 245 and 246.
Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule were held validly enacted to protect agrarian land reforms.
The provisional Parliament had full constitutional competence to enact constitutional amendments under Article 379.
Fundamental rights are not immune from constitutional amendment if the procedural requirements of Article 368 are satisfied.
This decision established the initial doctrine of parliamentary supremacy in constitutional amendment (later challenged in Sajjan Singh, Golak Nath, and Kesavananda).

provisions.title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution
provisions.relevance: Interpreted as conferring plenary constituent power unfettered by fundamental rights.

provisions.title: Prohibition against laws abridging fundamental rights
provisions.relevance: Held not to apply to constitutional amendments made under Article 368.

provisions.title: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations (Ninth Schedule)
provisions.relevance: Upheld as validly inserted to immunize agrarian land reforms from judicial challenge.

29.overview: Romesh Thappar, printer and publisher of the left-wing weekly journal 'Cross Roads' in Bombay, challenged an order of the Government of Madras banning the entry and circulation of his journal in the State under Section 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949.
29.issues: Whether the ban on the entry and circulation of a journal under the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act violates the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a).
29.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down the government order and Section 9(1-A) of the Act. The Court held that freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of circulation and propagation of ideas, which cannot be restricted on vague grounds of 'public safety'.
key_findings: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes not merely the right to publish, but crucially the right to circulate publications without state interference.
There can be no doubt that liberty of the press is an essential part of the right to freedom of speech and expression.
Unless a law strikes exclusively at activities directed against the security of the State or overthrow of the government, it cannot be sustained under Article 19(2).
'Public order' is distinct from and broader than 'security of the State'; restrictions based on general public safety were not authorized under the original text of Article 19(2).
A law that is drafted so widely as to permit restrictions beyond constitutional limits is void in its entirety and cannot be saved by severance.
Pre-censorship or circulation embargoes on printed literature are inherently suspect under democratic constitutionalism.
This decision prompted Parliament to enact the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951, inserting 'public order' into Article 19(2).

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to include freedom of press and the right of circulation and propagation of opinions.

provisions.title: Reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech
provisions.relevance: Strictly construed; original text did not include 'public order', invalidating the state ban.

provisions.title: Direct remedy before Supreme Court
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as a fundamental right; petitioner was not required to first approach the High Court under Article 226.

30.overview: The sons of Henry Golak Nath challenged the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, under which the State held that the family could only retain 30 acres each, with the surplus land being declared state property. The petitioners challenged the 1st, 4th, and 17th Constitutional Amendments which had placed the impugned Punjab Act in the Ninth Schedule.
30.issues: Whether Parliament has the constituent power under Article 368 to amend Part III of the Constitution and abrogate or take away fundamental rights, and whether an amendment is 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2).
30.holding: By a 6:5 majority, an 11-judge Constitution Bench overruled Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh, holding that Parliament cannot amend Part III of the Constitution to abridge or take away fundamental rights. The Court applied the doctrine of prospective overruling.
key_findings: Fundamental rights are primordial, transcendental, and inalienable human freedoms reserved to the people of India.
Article 368 merely contains the procedure for amendment, while the substantive power to amend is derived from the ordinary legislative power under Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I.
A constitutional amendment is 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2); consequently, an amendment that abridges fundamental rights is void.
Parliament has no constituent power outside the constitutional framework to abrogate or emasculate Part III fundamental rights.
To avoid chaotic invalidation of agrarian land reforms completed over 17 years, Chief Justice Subba Rao introduced the American doctrine of 'Prospective Overruling'.
The 1st, 4th, and 17th Amendments were held valid for past actions, but Parliament was forbidden from abridging fundamental rights in the future.
This decision led to the enactment of the 24th Amendment, setting the stage for the definitive showdown in Kesavananda Bharati.

provisions.title: Prohibition against laws taking away fundamental rights
provisions.relevance: Interpreted by the majority to encompass constitutional amendments under Article 368.

provisions.title: Procedure for amendment of the Constitution
provisions.relevance: Held to prescribe only procedural steps, not substantive sovereign constituent power to destroy rights.

provisions.title: Compulsory acquisition of property
provisions.relevance: Central to the property rights challenge that precipitated the constitutional clash over land reforms.

31.overview: Commander K.M. Nanavati, a naval officer, was tried for the murder of his wife's lover, Prem Ahuja. The Bombay sessions jury returned a verdict of 'not guilty' by an 8:1 majority, which the Sessions Judge referred to the High Court as perverse. The High Court convicted Nanavati of murder under Section 302 IPC. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, raising critical issues regarding grave and sudden provocation and jury trials.
31.issues: Whether the shooting of Prem Ahuja was committed under 'grave and sudden provocation' attracting Exception 1 to Section 300 IPC, and whether the Governor's suspension of sentence under Article 161 conflicted with the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 142.
31.holding: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction under Section 302 IPC and sentence of life imprisonment, holding that Nanavati had sufficient cooling time to reflect, negating grave and sudden provocation. The case led directly to the abolition of jury trials in India.
key_findings: To claim Exception 1 to Section 300 IPC, the fatal act must be committed while the accused is deprived of self-control by provocation that is both grave and sudden.
The test of grave and sudden provocation is whether a reasonable person placed in the accused's situation would be so overcome with passion as to lose self-control.
A lapse of three hours between discovering the confession and shooting Prem Ahuja provided ample cooling time to regain self-control.
The accused drove to naval headquarters, obtained a revolver under false pretenses, and proceeded to Ahuja's residence, demonstrating premeditation.
Jury verdicts that are perverse and unsupported by evidence can be referred and overturned by the High Court under Section 307 CrPC.
Under Article 161, the Governor's pardoning power cannot be exercised to suspend a sentence once the matter is sub judice before the Supreme Court under Article 142.
The public controversy and sensational jury verdict in this case led Parliament to abolish jury trials in the 1973 Code of Criminal Procedure.

provisions.title: Murder - Exception 1: Grave and sudden provocation
provisions.relevance: Authoritative interpretation of cooling time and premeditation defeating provocation defence.

provisions.title: Punishment for murder
provisions.relevance: Conviction and life imprisonment upheld based on proof of premeditated homicide.

provisions.title: Power of Governor to grant pardons
provisions.relevance: Harmonized with Article 142 to prevent executive interference with pending judicial appeals.

32.overview: During the Emergency declared under Article 352 in June 1975, the President issued an order under Article 359(1) suspending the right to move any court for the enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 21, and 22. Hundreds of political leaders and dissidents were detained without trial under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA). Multiple High Courts upheld habeas corpus petitions, prompting the Union Government to appeal to the Supreme Court.
32.issues: Whether, during the operation of a Presidential order under Article 359(1), a writ petition under Article 226 for habeas corpus challenging unlawful or mala fide detention is maintainable.
32.holding: By a 4:1 majority, the Supreme Court held that in view of the Presidential Order, no person had any locus standi to move a writ petition for habeas corpus to challenge an order of detention, even if mala fide or ultra vires. Justice H.R. Khanna delivered his legendary dissent.
key_findings: The majority held that Article 21 was the sole repository of the right to life and personal liberty against state action, and its suspension left citizens without legal remedy.
Courts were barred from reviewing the validity, legality, or bona fides of detention orders during the Emergency.
Justice H.R. Khanna delivered his immortal dissent, declaring that the right to life and liberty is not a gift of the Constitution but inherent in human existence.
Justice Khanna held that the rule of law is pervasive and invalidates executive detention without statutory authority even during Emergency.
The majority judgment is widely considered the darkest hour of Indian constitutional jurisprudence.
Parliament enacted the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, ensuring that Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended even during an Emergency.
In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), the 9-judge bench officially and unanimously overruled the majority opinion in ADM Jabalpur, adopting Justice Khanna's dissent.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Majority erroneously held it was the sole source of liberty; later overruled in Puttaswamy.

provisions.title: Suspension of enforcement of fundamental rights during emergencies
provisions.relevance: Interpreted by majority as totally extinguishing judicial review for habeas corpus.

provisions.title: Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
provisions.relevance: High Courts' habeas corpus jurisdiction was unconstitutionally silenced by the majority ruling.

33.overview: Sunil Batra, a prisoner sentenced to death in Tihar Jail, challenged his solitary confinement under Section 30(2) of the Prisons Act, 1894. A companion petition by Charles Sobhraj challenged the continuous imposition of bar fetters. The petitions raised the fundamental question of whether prisoners retain fundamental rights within prison walls.
33.issues: Whether prisoners retain fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21, and whether solitary confinement and bar fetters under the Prisons Act violate constitutional protections.
33.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that prisoners are not stripped of their fundamental rights upon incarceration. Section 30(2) of the Prisons Act was read down: solitary confinement can only be imposed after all judicial appeals are exhausted and the death sentence is final.
key_findings: Prisoners do not become non-persons; fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21 accompany convicts into prison walls.
Imprisonment involves loss of liberty to roam, but not loss of human dignity, bodily integrity, and mental autonomy.
Section 30(2) of the Prisons Act, which provides for keeping a prisoner under sentence of death 'in a cell apart from all other prisoners', does not authorize solitary confinement.
Solitary confinement produces severe mental agony and dehumanization and can only be imposed in accordance with judicial sentence under Sections 73 and 74 IPC.
Imposition of bar fetters and physical restraints on prisoners without objective security justification violates Article 21.
Prison administrators cannot inflict inhuman, cruel, or degrading punishment without prior judicial sanction.
The Supreme Court established judicial oversight over prison conditions through epistolary jurisdiction and prison inspection mechanisms.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as extending behind prison walls to protect convicts from cruel and degrading treatment.

provisions.title: Prisoners under sentence of death
provisions.relevance: Read down to exclude solitary confinement prior to final confirmation of death sentence.

provisions.title: Confinement in irons
provisions.relevance: Subjected to strict judicial control to prevent routine bar-fettering of undertrials and convicts.

34.overview: Advocate Kapila Hingorani filed a PIL under Article 32 based on investigative newspaper reports in the Indian Express detailing the horrific plight of thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar jails who had been incarcerated for periods far exceeding the maximum sentence for their alleged offences.
34.issues: Whether the right to a speedy trial is an integral facet of fundamental personal liberty under Article 21, and whether the State has a constitutional obligation to provide free legal aid to impoverished undertrials.
34.holding: The Supreme Court held that the right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Article 21. The Court ordered the immediate release of thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar and established state-funded legal aid as a constitutional mandate.
key_findings: Expeditious trial is an integral and essential part of the 'just, fair, and reasonable' procedure established by law under Article 21.
Undertrials cannot be allowed to languish in jail indefinitely due to systemic judicial delays, administrative lethargy, or inability to furnish bail.
Prolonged pre-trial detention that exceeds the maximum sentence punishable for the offence violates Articles 14 and 21.
The State is under a constitutional mandate under Article 21 and Article 39A to provide free legal services to indigent accused at state expense.
A trial court cannot validly proceed with a criminal trial without offering legal representation to an accused who cannot afford counsel.
This historic decision marked the true dawn of Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India, spearheaded by advocate Kapila Hingorani and Justice P.N. Bhagwati.
The Court ordered comprehensive undertrial census and automatic release mechanisms for prisoners detained without chargesheets.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass the fundamental right to a speedy trial and humane pre-trial procedure.

provisions.title: Equal justice and free legal aid
provisions.relevance: Integrated into Article 21 to create an enforceable state duty to provide free legal counsel to the poor.

provisions.title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours
provisions.relevance: Enforced to prevent indefinite detention without filing of police final reports.

35.overview: Minerva Mills, a textile company in Bangalore, was taken over by the Central Government under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974. The company challenged the takeover along with Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, which had declared Parliament's amending power under Article 368 unlimited and elevated all Directive Principles above Fundamental Rights.
35.issues: Whether Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment Act violate the Basic Structure Doctrine by conferring unlimited amending power on Parliament and destroying the supremacy of fundamental rights.
35.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment Act as unconstitutional. The Court held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature of the Constitution, and that harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential constitutional pillar.
key_findings: A limited amending power under Article 368 is itself a basic feature of the Constitution; Parliament cannot use a limited power to enlarge it into absolute power.
Section 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which inserted clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368 barring judicial review of amendments, was struck down for destroying judicial review.
Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment, which amended Article 31C to insulate any law giving effect to any Directive Principle from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, was held unconstitutional.
The Constitution is founded on the bedrock of balance and harmony between Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles).
To give absolute primacy to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights is to disturb the harmony that constitutes the basic structure of the Constitution.
Judicial review is a vital constitutional mechanism to prevent legislative and executive transgressions of constitutional boundaries.

Chief Justice Chandrachud poetically observed: 'The Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Parts III and IV. To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution.'

provisions.title: Clauses barring judicial review of constitutional amendments
provisions.relevance: Struck down as unconstitutional for destroying judicial review and the basic structure.

provisions.title: Saving of laws giving effect to Directive Principles
provisions.relevance: The blanket protection extended by the 42nd Amendment was invalidated for obliterating Articles 14 and 19.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as an indispensable fundamental right that cannot be subordinated wholesale to Directive Principles.

36.overview: Bandhua Mukti Morcha, an organization dedicated to eradicating bonded labour, addressed a letter to the Supreme Court detailing inhuman working conditions of stone quarry workers in Faridabad, Haryana. Workers were held in debt bondage, denied potable water, forced to live in unhygienic huts, and exposed to occupational hazards without medical care.
36.issues: Whether bonded labour violates Article 21 and Article 23, and whether epistolary petitions filed by public-spirited citizens on behalf of exploited workers are maintainable under Article 32.
36.holding: The Supreme Court recognized epistolary jurisdiction under Article 32, treated the letter as a writ petition, and issued comprehensive directives to identify, release, and rehabilitate bonded labourers. The Court held that the right to live under Article 21 includes the right to live with human dignity.
key_findings: Article 21 derives its life breath from the Directive Principles; it guarantees the right to live with human dignity, free from exploitation.
The right to life includes basic necessities: adequate nutrition, clothing, shelter, educational facilities, and humane working conditions.
Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar, and other similar forms of forced labour; forced labour exists whenever a person is paid less than minimum wage or denied freedom of movement.
Epistolary jurisdiction under Article 32 permits courts to waive procedural formalities and treat simple letters as writ petitions on behalf of poor, disadvantaged citizens.
The Court appointed socio-legal commissioners to investigate quarry conditions and report directly to the Supreme Court.
District Magistrates have an active statutory duty under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 to identify, release, and provide economic rehabilitation.
State inaction in eradicating bonded labour constitutes a direct violation of constitutional obligations.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Expanded to encompass human dignity and basic economic survival rights for exploited labourers.

provisions.title: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
provisions.relevance: Directly enforced to abolish debt bondage and unremunerative quarry labour.

provisions.title: Remedies for enforcement of rights
provisions.relevance: Formally developed as epistolary public interest litigation accessible to public-spirited NGOs.

provisions.title: Entire Act
provisions.relevance: Mandatorily enforced against state authorities and private quarry mine operators.

37.overview: Shah Bano Begum, a 62-year-old Muslim woman with five children, was divorced by her husband Mohd. Ahmed Khan, an advocate. The husband paid her mahr (Rs 3,000) and maintenance during iddat, then refused further financial support, contending that under Muslim personal law, a husband has no obligation to maintain a divorced wife beyond the iddat period.
37.issues: Whether Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to Muslim divorced women, and whether the payment of mahr or iddat maintenance extinguishes a husband's liability under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.
37.holding: A unanimous 5-judge Constitution Bench held that Section 125 CrPC is a secular, social-justice measure that applies to all Indian citizens regardless of religion. A divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself is entitled to maintenance from her former husband beyond the iddat period.
key_findings: Section 125 CrPC is a secular procedural provision designed to prevent destitution and vagrancy; it operates independently of personal laws.

There is no conflict between Section 125 CrPC and Islamic personal law; the Holy Quran (Surah Al-Baqarah, Ayat 241-242) imposes an obligation on husbands to provide reasonable maintenance (mata) to divorced women.
Mahr is an obligation imposed on the husband as a mark of respect for the wife and does not represent an amount payable 'on divorce' within the meaning of Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.
Payment of mahr does not absolve the husband of his liability under Section 125 if the divorced wife is unable to maintain herself.
A secular criminal procedure code cannot permit discriminatory loopholes that leave destitute women without economic support.
Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud emphasized the constitutional goal of a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44 to promote national integration and gender justice.
The political backlash against the ruling prompted Parliament to enact the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.

provisions.title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents
provisions.relevance: Held to be a secular social welfare remedy overriding personal law limitations.

provisions.title: Alteration in allowance on payment of customary sum
provisions.relevance: Interpreted strictly: payment of mahr does not extinguish ongoing maintenance liability.

provisions.title: Uniform Civil Code
provisions.relevance: Highlighted by the Court as an unfulfilled constitutional directive essential for gender justice.

38.overview: Shortly after the Bhopal Gas Disaster, a major leak of oleum gas occurred from the caustic chlorine plant of Shriram Foods and Fertilizers Industries in a densely populated area of Delhi, causing panic and the death of an advocate. Environmentalist lawyer M.C. Mehta filed an application under Article 32 seeking the closure of the hazardous industry and compensation for victims.
38.issues: What is the scope of liability of enterprises engaged in hazardous and inherently dangerous activities, and whether the Supreme Court has the power under Article 32 to award compensation for environmental disasters.
38.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench propounded the historic 'Absolute Liability' principle, holding that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an absolute, non-delegable duty to the community, subject to none of the exceptions of the strict liability rule in Rylands v. Fletcher.
key_findings: The 19th-century English rule of strict liability in Rylands v. Fletcher (subject to exceptions like act of God, sabotage, plaintiff's consent) is inadequate for modern industrial conditions.
An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute, non-delegable duty to ensure no harm results to anyone.
If damage occurs from a hazardous activity, the enterprise is strictly and absolutely liable to compensate all affected persons without any defence.
The measure of compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise to have a real deterrent effect (deeper the pockets, greater the compensation).
The power of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is not confined to issuing traditional writs; it encompasses the power to award compensation for violations of Article 21.
The Court permitted the plant to restart under strict conditions, including continuous monitoring, safety audits, and personal undertaking from management.
This decision created the foundation for modern Indian environmental jurisprudence and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to include the right to a clean, safe, and hazard-free environment.

provisions.title: Remedies for enforcement of fundamental rights
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as authorizing the Supreme Court to grant compensatory remedies for environmental torts.

provisions.title: Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests
provisions.relevance: Applied as a constitutional guiding principle for state industrial regulation.

39.overview: The Union Government issued office memoranda implementing the recommendations of the Second Backward Classes Commission (Mandal Commission), providing 27% reservation in central civil posts and services for Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs/OBCs). The notification was challenged in the Supreme Court by student associations, bar councils, and general category candidates.
39.issues: Whether caste can be the primary criterion for identifying backward classes under Article 16(4), whether reservations can exceed 50%, whether reservations apply to promotions, and what is the role of the 'creamy layer'.
39.holding: A 9-judge Constitution Bench (6:3 majority) upheld the 27% reservation for OBCs under Article 16(4), subject to the exclusion of the 'creamy layer'. The Court ruled that total reservations cannot exceed 50% except in extraordinary circumstances, and reservations do not apply to promotions.
key_findings: Caste can be an important and starting point for identifying backward classes under Article 16(4), provided social and educational backwardness is demonstrated.
The 'creamy layer' (socially and economically advanced members of backward classes) must be strictly excluded from the benefits of reservation to ensure benefits reach the truly needy.
Total reservations under Article 16(4) must not exceed 50% in a given year, absent extraordinary situations in remote and far-flung territories.
Reservation is restricted to initial appointments and does not apply to promotions in public employment (subsequently amended by 77th and 85th Amendments).
Article 16(4) is not an exception to Article 16(1), but an emphatic restatement of the facet of substantive equality.
Backward classes under Article 16(4) are not identical to socially and educationally backward classes in Article 15(4); economic criteria alone cannot determine backwardness under Article 16(4).
State and Central Governments were directed to constitute permanent statutory commissions (National Commission for Backward Classes) to examine additions and deletions.

provisions.title: Reservation in appointments for backward classes
provisions.relevance: Foundational provision interpreted to uphold 27% OBC quota while instituting the 50% ceiling and creamy layer exclusion.

provisions.title: Equality of opportunity in public employment
provisions.relevance: Harmonized with Article 16(4) under the doctrine of proportionate substantive equality.

provisions.title: Appointment of a Commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes
provisions.relevance: Constitutional authority under which the Mandal Commission was originally constituted.

40.overview: The Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and senior lawyers challenged the executive's dominance in judicial appointments and transfers following the First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta, 1981), which had held that 'consultation' did not mean 'concurrence' and that executive had final say. A 9-judge Constitution Bench was constituted to re-evaluate the constitutional scheme of judicial appointments.
40.issues: Whether the executive or the judiciary holds primacy in the appointment of judges to the High Courts and Supreme Court under Articles 124(2) and 217(1), and whether 'consultation' with the Chief Justice of India implies 'concurrence'.
40.holding: A 9-judge Constitution Bench (7:2 majority) overruled S.P. Gupta (First Judges Case) and established the primacy of the Chief Justice of India in judicial appointments. The Court created the 'Collegium System', holding that 'consultation' requires effective concurrence based on the collective view of the CJI and senior colleagues.
key_findings: Independence of the judiciary is an inviolable basic feature of the Constitution, which requires that judicial appointments be insulated from executive control.
The term 'consultation' in Articles 124(2) and 217(1) must be interpreted as 'concurrence' in the constitutional context of judicial appointments.
The Chief Justice of India holds primacy in the appointment process, ensuring that executive veto over judicial selections is eliminated.
The opinion of the Chief Justice of India is not his individual subjective opinion, but a collective institutional view formed after consulting the two senior-most judges of the Supreme Court.
No appointment to the Supreme Court or High Courts can be made unless it conforms to the opinion of the CJI-led Collegium.
The executive retains the power to seek reconsideration for strong recorded reasons, but if the Collegium reiterates its recommendation unanimously, the appointment is binding.
Seniority among High Court Chief Justices is an important criterion for Supreme Court elevations, though merit and regional representation are relevant.

provisions.title: Appointment of Supreme Court judges
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to establish that 'consultation' with the CJI means binding concurrence and judicial primacy.

provisions.title: Appointment and conditions of High Court judges
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to require mandatory primacy of the judicial Collegium in High Court appointments.

provisions.title: Transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another
provisions.relevance: Subjected to strict Collegium consultation to prevent punitive executive transfers.

41.overview: Following the dismissal of state governments in Karnataka, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Himachal Pradesh by the President under Article 356, state Chief Ministers, led by S.R. Bommai, challenged the proclamations as mala fide, arbitrary, and violative of federalism. A 9-judge Constitution Bench was constituted to settle the scope of judicial review over Presidential rule.
41.issues: Whether a Presidential proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, what constitutes 'breakdown of constitutional machinery', whether secularism is part of the basic structure, and whether the floor test is mandatory.
41.holding: A 9-judge Constitution Bench held that a proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review. The Court held that secularism and federalism are basic features of the Constitution, and that a floor test on the floor of the Legislative Assembly is the only constitutionally valid method to test a government's majority.
key_findings: Proclamations under Article 356 are subject to judicial review; courts can examine whether relevant material existed and whether executive power was exercised mala fide.
Secularism is an inviolable basic feature of the Constitution; political parties cannot use religion for electoral mobilization or subvert secular governance.
Federalism is a core pillar of the basic structure; the Central Government cannot dismiss elected state governments arbitrarily or for political convenience.
The floor of the House is the only constitutionally permissible arena to test whether an incumbent Ministry commands the confidence of the Legislative Assembly.
A State Assembly cannot be dissolved prematurely merely upon issuing an Article 356 proclamation; dissolution is permissible only after both Houses of Parliament approve the proclamation.
If an Article 356 proclamation is held unconstitutional, the Court has the power under Article 142 to restore the dismissed state government and revive the dissolved Legislative Assembly.
The Governor's subjective report cannot substitute for an objective floor test except in extraordinary conditions of total lawlessness.

provisions.title: Provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States
provisions.relevance: Subordinated to judicial review and strictly circumscribed to prevent abuse of federal balance.

provisions.title: Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance
provisions.relevance: Interpreted as setting the threshold condition precedent for invoking Article 356.

provisions.title: Secularism
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as a fundamental basic structure principle justifying state dismissal if secularism is subverted.

42.overview: Four women filed writ petitions in the Supreme Court pointing out that their Hindu husbands had converted to Islam solely for the purpose of contracting a second marriage without legally divorcing their first wives under the Hindu Marriage Act. The husbands claimed that conversion entitled them to have four wives under Muslim personal law, leaving first wives without legal redress.
42.issues: Whether a Hindu husband, married under Hindu law, can solemnize a second marriage by simply embracing Islam without dissolving his first marriage, and whether such second marriage is void under Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code.
