42.holding: A 2-judge Bench held that a marriage solemnized under Hindu law continues to subsist until dissolved by a decree of divorce under the Hindu Marriage Act. Conversion to Islam does not dissolve the first marriage, and a second marriage contracted during the subsistence of the first is void and punishable under Section 494 IPC.
key_findings: A marriage solemnized under personal law creates a legal status that cannot be extinguished by the unilateral apostasy or religious conversion of one party.
A Hindu marriage can be dissolved only on grounds recognized under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; conversion does not automatically dissolve the marital tie.
A second marriage contracted by a Hindu husband during the subsistence of his first marriage, even after embracing Islam, is bigamous and void in law.
The husband committing bigamy under the garb of conversion is liable to criminal prosecution and conviction under Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code.
Conversion undertaken purely for fraudulent circumvention of penal law and civil obligations constitutes an abuse of religious freedom under Article 25.
Justice Kuldip Singh strongly urged the Government of India to enact a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44 to protect women from bigamous exploitation.
Reiterated the constitutional principle of gender equality prohibiting patriarchal evasion of marital duties.

provisions.title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife (Bigamy)
provisions.relevance: Directly applied to hold converting husbands criminally liable for contracting second marriages.

provisions.title: Void marriages and divorce grounds
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to establish that Hindu marriage continues to subsist until dissolved by competent court decree.

provisions.title: Uniform Civil Code
provisions.relevance: Judicially invoked to advocate for uniform personal laws safeguarding women's rights.

43.overview: The Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum filed a PIL under Article 32 highlighting catastrophic ecological devastation caused by untreated chemical trade effluents discharged by tanneries and industrial units in the Palar river basin in Tamil Nadu. The toxic effluents contaminated groundwater, spoiled agricultural lands, and deprived tens of thousands of residents of potable drinking water.
43.issues: Whether commercial industrial operations can be permitted to pollute river basins causing severe health hazards, and how the Precautionary Principle and the Polluter Pays Principle apply to sustainable development in India.
43.holding: A 3-judge Bench incorporated the 'Precautionary Principle' and the 'Polluter Pays Principle' as essential components of Indian environmental law under Article 21. The Court ordered the closure of non-compliant tanneries and directed the creation of an environmental authority to assess and levy compensation.
key_findings: The Precautionary Principle and the Polluter Pays Principle are essential features of Sustainable Development and form an integral part of customary international law accepted into Indian municipal law.

Under the Precautionary Principle, state authorities must anticipate, prevent, and attack the causes of environmental degradation; lack of full scientific certainty cannot justify postponing preventive measures.
The onus of proof is on the industrialist or developer to show that their commercial actions are environmentally benign.
Under the Polluter Pays Principle, the absolute financial liability for reversing the environmental damage and compensating affected villagers rests squarely on the polluting enterprise.
Industrial development and ecological balance must be harmonized under sustainable development; economic growth cannot be achieved by sacrificing human health.
The Court directed the Madras High Court to constitute a special 'Green Bench' to continuously monitor environmental compliance across Tamil Nadu.
The Central Government was directed to establish an authority under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 with power to compute damages.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass the fundamental human right to a pollution-free environment and safe drinking water.

provisions.title: Power to establish authorities
provisions.relevance: Enforced to establish a specialized statutory tribunal for determining environmental damages in the Palar basin.

provisions.title: Environmental protection directives and duties
provisions.relevance: Applied as foundational constitutional principles to interpret statutory environmental mandates.

44.overview: Prakash Singh, former Director General of the Border Security Force (BSF) and former DGP of Uttar Pradesh, filed a PIL under Article 32 alongside other retired senior police officers. The petition highlighted deep-rooted systemic political interference, corruption, arbitrary transfers, and lack of accountability in the police apparatus, urging the Court to implement overdue police reforms.
44.issues: Whether police forces can be insulated from political interference to secure the rule of law, and what institutional mechanisms are required to ensure police autonomy, tenure security, and professional accountability.
44.holding: The Supreme Court issued seven historic, binding directives to the Central and State Governments to enact police reforms across India, mandating State Security Commissions, fixed minimum tenures for senior officers, separation of investigation from law and order, and Police Complaints Authorities.
key_findings: The rule of law is severely imperiled when law enforcement agencies function as instruments of political parties rather than guardians of the Constitution.
Directive 1: State Security Commission (SSC) must be established in every state to lay down policy guidelines and evaluate police performance free from partisan pressure.
Directive 2: Director General of Police (DGP) must be selected through transparent UPSC empanelment and granted a guaranteed minimum tenure of at least two years.
Directive 3: Police officers on operational duties (IG, DIG, SP, SHO) must be provided a minimum tenure of two years to insulate them from punitive transfers.
Directive 4: Separation of investigative staff from law and order personnel in all major urban police stations to ensure speedy, professional investigation.
Directive 5: Police Establishment Board (PEB) must be created in every state to decide transfers, postings, and promotions of officers below the rank of SP.
Directive 6 & 7: Police Complaints Authorities (PCA) must be set up at State and District levels headed by retired judges to investigate serious police misconduct and custodial abuse.

provisions.title: Inherent constitutional powers for complete justice
provisions.relevance: Invoked to issue binding directives to all States and Union Territories in the absence of updated police legislation.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as requiring an impartial, professional, and accountable police force to protect citizens from crime and state oppression.

provisions.title: Colonial police framework
provisions.relevance: Identified as an archaic colonial statute requiring urgent structural modernization.

45.overview: Following the ruling in Kesavananda Bharati, Parliament continued to place numerous land, economic, and social statutes into the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B to immunize them from judicial review under Part III. A 9-judge Constitution Bench was constituted in I.R. Coelho to conclusively resolve whether Ninth Schedule laws remained subject to judicial review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure Doctrine.
45.issues: Whether laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after the judgment in Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973) are immune from judicial challenge, or whether they can be invalidated for violating fundamental rights that form part of the basic structure.
45.holding: A unanimous 9-judge Constitution Bench held that all constitutional amendments and statutory enactments included in the Ninth Schedule on or after 24 April 1973 do not enjoy blanket immunity. If any such law violates fundamental rights that form part of the basic structure of the Constitution, it will be struck down.
key_findings: The Ninth Schedule does not create a constitutional black hole or enclave beyond the reach of judicial review.
The cutoff date is 24 April 1973 (date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment); laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before this date are protected, but laws inserted thereafter are subject to review.
Judicial review is a basic feature of the Constitution; Parliament cannot defeat it by the simple expedient of placing statutes in the Ninth Schedule.
The validity of Ninth Schedule laws must be tested using the 'Rights Test' and the 'Essence of Rights Test' on the touchstone of the basic structure doctrine.
If the application of a Ninth Schedule statute destroys or damages core fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, or 21, the amendment inserting it into the Ninth Schedule is void.
The constituent power of Parliament under Article 368 cannot be exercised to bypass constitutional supremacy and destroy the constitutional framework through Article 31B.
Affirmed the ultimate supremacy of fundamental human rights over unlimited statutory immunities.

provisions.title: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations (Ninth Schedule)
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to hold that laws inserted post-24 April 1973 are subject to the Basic Structure Doctrine.

provisions.title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution
provisions.relevance: Reaffirmed that amending power cannot be used to insulate unconstitutional statutes from judicial scrutiny.

provisions.title: The Golden Triangle Fundamental Rights
provisions.relevance: Identified as core pillars of the basic structure against which Ninth Schedule laws must be measured.

46.overview: Criminal investigating agencies increasingly subjected accused persons and suspects to modern neuro-scientific techniques—narco-analysis (sodium pentothal truth serum), polygraph (lie-detector) tests, and Brain Electrical Activation Profiling (BEAP / P-300 brain mapping)—without their consent. Smt. Selvi and other accused challenged the involuntary administration of these techniques under Article 32.
46.issues: Whether the involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph tests, and brain mapping violates the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and the right to privacy and personal liberty under Article 21.
46.holding: A unanimous 3-judge Bench held that the involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph examination, and brain electrical activation profiling violates the privilege against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and the right to privacy and mental autonomy under Article 21. No individual can be subjected to such techniques without consent.
key_findings: The right against self-incrimination in Article 20(3) protects an individual's right to remain silent and not to be compelled to give testimony against themselves.
Involuntary administration of neuro-scientific techniques involves physical and psychological coercion to extract statements, directly violating Article 20(3).
The constitutional guarantee under Article 20(3) applies not merely to courtroom trials, but from the very stage of police investigation and interrogation.
Involuntary intrusion into the mental privacy and subconscious mind of an individual violates bodily and psychological integrity protected under Article 21.
Statements made under the influence of narco-analysis or polygraph cannot be admitted as evidence in a court of law.
However, if any physical object, document, or material evidence is subsequently discovered pursuant to voluntary testing, that fact may be admitted under Section 27 Evidence Act.
Voluntary administration is permitted only if accompanied by strict procedural safeguards, including informed consent before a Judicial Magistrate and legal representation.

provisions.title: Right against self-incrimination
provisions.relevance: Enforced to hold that involuntary narco-analysis and lie-detector tests constitute unconstitutional testimonial compulsion.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to protect mental privacy, psychological integrity, and bodily autonomy from state intrusion.

provisions.title: Information leading to discovery of fact
provisions.relevance: Limited strictly to material discoveries pursuant to voluntary testing, excluding testimonial statements.

47.overview: Following controversial arrests of citizens across India for posting political comments and cartoons on social media under Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, law student Shreya Singhal, alongside civil liberties organizations, filed a PIL under Article 32 challenging Section 66A as vague, overbroad, and unconstitutional.
47.issues: Whether Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 violates the fundamental freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), and whether it is saved by the reasonable restrictions in Article 19(2).
47.holding: A 2-judge Bench struck down Section 66A of the IT Act in its entirety as unconstitutional and void for being overbroad, vague, and having a chilling effect on online speech. The Court held that speech on the internet enjoys the same constitutional protection under Article 19(1)(a) as speech in print or oral form.
key_findings: Section 66A criminalized online communications that were 'grossly offensive' or caused 'annoyance', terms that were undefined, vague, and subject to subjective police manipulation.

The Court drew a vital constitutional distinction between 'discussion', 'advocacy', and 'incitement'; only speech that reaches the level of incitement to violence or clear public disorder can be restricted under Article 19(2).
Section 66A suffered from the vice of overbreadth, sweeping within its net innocent, humorous, and constitutionally protected free speech.
The provision created an insidious 'chilling effect' on legitimate public discourse, political criticism, and artistic expression on the internet.
Section 66A had no proximate or rational nexus to any of the permissible heads of restriction enumerated in Article 19(2) (public order, security of state, etc.).

Section 79(3)(b) (intermediary safe harbour) was read down to mean that online intermediaries are only required to block or takedown content upon receiving a court order or authorized government notification.
Section 69A of the IT Act and the blocking rules were upheld subject to procedural safeguards and written reasoned orders.

provisions.title: Punishment for sending offensive messages through communication service
provisions.relevance: Struck down in its entirety as unconstitutional and violative of Article 19(1)(a).

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression
provisions.relevance: Applied to protect digital and internet expression with the same constitutional vigour as traditional print and speech.

provisions.title: Reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech
provisions.relevance: Strictly construed to hold that vague notions of annoyance cannot qualify as restrictions under public order.

provisions.title: Exemption from liability of intermediary
provisions.relevance: Read down so that intermediaries only take down content upon judicial or governmental directions.

48.overview: Parliament enacted the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act, 2014 to replace the Collegium system. The NJAC comprised the Chief Justice of India, two senior SC judges, the Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons. The Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and others challenged the package as an assault on judicial independence.
48.issues: Whether the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and the NJAC Act violate the Basic Structure Doctrine by compromising the independence of the judiciary and separation of powers.
48.holding: By a 4:1 majority, a 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and the NJAC Act, 2014 in their entirety as unconstitutional and void. The Court revived the Collegium system, holding that judicial independence is a basic feature of the Constitution requiring judicial primacy.
key_findings: Independence of the judiciary and separation of powers are non-negotiable basic features of the Constitution of India.
Judicial primacy in the appointment of higher judiciary judges is an indispensable component of judicial independence.

The inclusion of the Union Law Minister as a member of the Commission gave the executive a direct voice and potential veto over the appointment of judges who adjudicate cases against the government (the biggest litigant).

The provision enabling any two members of the NJAC to veto a judicial nomination meant that the two 'eminent persons' (appointed with executive participation) could override the unanimous recommendation of the Chief Justice and judges.
The NJAC scheme severely undermined the institutional autonomy of the judiciary and exposed appointments to political bartering.
The striking down of the 99th Amendment automatically revived the pre-existing Collegium system established in the Second and Third Judges cases.
Justice J. Chelameswar delivered a dissenting opinion defending the constitutional validity of the NJAC while calling for greater transparency.

provisions.title: Establishment of the National Judicial Appointments Commission
provisions.relevance: Struck down as unconstitutional for destroying judicial independence and the basic structure.

provisions.title: NJAC framework inserted by 99th Amendment
provisions.relevance: Declared void in their entirety, restoring the original text of Articles 124 and 217.

provisions.title: Separation of judiciary from executive
provisions.relevance: Emphasized as the constitutional bedrock supporting institutional judicial independence.

49.overview: Operational creditors, promoters of defaulting corporate debtors, and trade associations challenged the constitutional validity of several provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. Petitioners alleged arbitrary classification between financial and operational creditors, exclusion of promoters under Section 29A, and excessive tribunals powers under Article 14.
49.issues: Whether the classification between financial creditors and operational creditors under the IBC violates Article 14, and whether Section 29A disqualifying defaulting promoters from bidding is unconstitutional.
49.holding: A 2-judge Bench upheld the constitutional validity of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 in its entirety, affirming that economic legislation must be granted legislative deference and that the distinct treatment of financial creditors has a rational nexus to corporate revival.
key_findings: Economic statutes must be evaluated with judicial deference; the legislature is free to experiment in economic matters without courts acting as super-legislatures.
The classification between financial creditors (banks/lenders who assess viability from inception) and operational creditors (goods/services suppliers) is intelligible and rational under Article 14.
Financial creditors are in a far superior position to formulate and vote on corporate resolution plans aimed at keeping the debtor as a going concern.
Section 29A, which bars defaulting promoters who brought the company to insolvency from bidding for the corporate debtor, is fully valid and prevents unscrupulous recapture.
The primary objective of the IBC is corporate reorganization and maximizing asset value, with liquidation being only a last resort.
The speed and discipline enforced by statutory timelines under the IBC represent a vital economic reform to restore banking system health.
The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) was designated as the exclusive appellate forum, insulating commercial resolution from civil court injunctions.

provisions.title: Entire Code (specifically Sections 5(7), 5(20), 21, 29A)
provisions.relevance: Upheld as constitutionally valid, setting the gold standard for Indian insolvency jurisprudence.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied with economic deference to validate the statutory distinction between financial and operational creditors.

provisions.title: Persons not eligible to be resolution applicant
provisions.relevance: Upheld as a constitutional prophylactic measure against defaulting promoters regaining control.

50.overview: NGO Common Cause filed a PIL under Article 32 praying for the declaration that the right to die with dignity is an inseparable facet of the right to life under Article 21, and seeking judicial recognition for 'Advance Medical Directives' (Living Wills) allowing individuals suffering from terminal illnesses to refuse vegetative life support.
50.issues: Whether the right to life with dignity under Article 21 includes the right to die with dignity, and whether passive euthanasia and advance medical directives (living wills) should be recognized under Indian law.
50.holding: A unanimous 5-judge Constitution Bench held that the right to die with dignity is a fundamental right under Article 21. The Court granted legal recognition to passive euthanasia and advance medical directives (living wills), framing comprehensive guidelines to regulate their execution and implementation.
key_findings: The right to life under Article 21 is not mere animal existence; it encompasses the fundamental human right to lead a dignified life until the point of death.
A person with capacity has the constitutional right to bodily integrity, personal autonomy, and the right to refuse medical treatment or life support.
Passive euthanasia (withholding or withdrawing medical treatment and artificial life support to allow death in natural course) is legally recognized.
Active euthanasia (positive lethal intervention) remains illegal and constitutes an offence under Indian penal law.
Adults of sound mind can execute an 'Advance Medical Directive' (Living Will) specifying that life support not be prolonged in the event of vegetative irreversibility.
The decision in Gian Kaur (1996) was clarified: while Article 21 does not include an unnatural right to extinguish life (suicide), it includes the right to a dignified natural death.
The Court laid down a multi-tier medical board procedure to certify that a patient is in a permanent vegetative state before withdrawing life support.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass individual autonomy, bodily self-determination, and the right to die with dignity.

provisions.title: Enforcement of decrees and orders of Supreme Court
provisions.relevance: Invoked to formulate binding nationwide procedural guidelines for Living Wills pending parliamentary legislation.

51.overview: A landlord filed an eviction petition against a tenant under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The tenancy agreement contained an arbitration clause, but following the Supreme Court's earlier ruling in Himangni Enterprises, eviction disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act were considered non-arbitrable. A 3-judge Bench was constituted to settle the test of subject-matter arbitrability under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
51.issues: What is the test to determine whether a civil dispute is arbitrable under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and whether tenancy disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act are capable of being settled by arbitration.
51.holding: A 3-judge Bench overruled Himangni Enterprises and laid down a comprehensive four-fold test to determine subject-matter arbitrability. The Court held that landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable unless covered by special rent control legislation.
key_findings: Arbitrability must be tested using a comprehensive four-fold test (the Vidya Drolia Test).
A dispute is non-arbitrable when: (1) it relates to actions in rem (rights against the world) rather than in personam; (2) it affects third-party rights or requires centralized adjudication.
A dispute is non-arbitrable when: (3) it relates to inalienable sovereign functions of the State; or (4) it is expressly or implicitly excluded by statute creating a special public court/tribunal.
Disputes between landlords and tenants under the Transfer of Property Act relate to rights in personam and are fully capable of being resolved by arbitration.
However, if a tenancy is governed by a special statutory rent control legislation conferring exclusive jurisdiction on Rent Controllers, arbitration is excluded.
At the referral stage under Section 8 and Section 11 of the Arbitration Act, judicial examination is limited to a prima facie review of the existence of the arbitration agreement.
The arbitral tribunal is the preferred primary forum under Section 16 (competence-competence) to decide complex questions of arbitrability and jurisdiction.

provisions.title: Power to refer parties to arbitration and appointment of arbitrators
provisions.relevance: Judicial review at the referral stage restricted to a prima facie verification of the arbitration agreement.

provisions.title: Competence of arbitral tribunal to rule on its jurisdiction
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as the primary rule conferring jurisdiction on the arbitrator to decide arbitrability.

provisions.title: Chapter V: Leases
provisions.relevance: Eviction and rent disputes under general law held fully arbitrable.

52.overview: Following the revocation of the special constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 in August 2019, the Union Government imposed severe restrictions on movement under Section 144 CrPC and shut down all internet and telecommunication services across the region. Anuradha Bhasin, executive editor of the Kashmir Times, challenged the indefinite internet shutdown under Article 32.
52.issues: Whether the indefinite shutdown of the internet and telecommunications violates fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), and whether orders imposing such restrictions are subject to judicial review.
52.holding: A 3-judge Bench held that freedom of speech and expression and the right to carry on trade and commerce over the medium of the internet are constitutionally protected under Article 19(1)(a) and Article 19(1)(g). The Court ruled that indefinite suspension of internet services is impermissible in law.
key_findings: The freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to practice any profession or trade over the medium of the internet are protected under Article 19(1)(a) and Article 19(1)(g).
Any restriction on internet access must satisfy the constitutional requirements of necessity and proportionality under Article 19(2) and Article 19(6).
An indefinite suspension of internet services is contrary to the law; suspension can only be temporary under the Suspension of Telecom Services Rules, 2017.
All suspension orders under Section 144 CrPC and Telecom Suspension Rules must be published and made publicly accessible to enable affected citizens to seek judicial review.
Orders under Section 144 CrPC cannot be used as a routine administrative tool to suppress the legitimate expression of opinion, grievance, or democratic assembly.
A Review Committee must periodically review all internet suspension orders every seven days to determine whether the continuation of restrictions remains justified.
The Government of India was directed to immediately review all orders suspending internet services in Jammu & Kashmir.

provisions.title: Freedoms of speech and trade over internet
provisions.relevance: Explicitly recognized as extending to digital communications and online commerce.

provisions.title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or danger
provisions.relevance: Subjected to strict proportionality oversight to prevent routine democratic suppression.

provisions.title: Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services Rules
provisions.relevance: Indefinite orders held ultra vires; mandatory periodic review instituted.

53.overview: The Governor of Punjab withheld assent to several bills passed by the Punjab Legislative Assembly, including financial bills, on the pretext that the assembly sitting called by the Speaker was illegal. The State of Punjab filed a writ petition under Article 32 challenging the Governor's inaction, arguing that the constitutional machinery was paralyzed by the Governor's refusal to act on bills.
53.issues: What are the constitutional limits of a Governor's power under Article 200 of the Constitution, and whether a Governor can withhold assent to bills passed by an elected state legislature indefinitely.
53.holding: A 3-judge Bench headed by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud held that the Governor cannot sit on bills passed by the State Legislature indefinitely. Under Article 200, the Governor is a constitutional figurehead and must act on bills with dispatch; if assent is withheld, the bill must be returned immediately to the Legislature.
key_findings: In a parliamentary democracy, real executive power resides in the elected Council of Ministers; the Governor cannot act as an unelected veto over the legislative process.
Under Article 200, the Governor has only three constitutional choices: grant assent, withhold assent, or reserve the bill for the President's consideration.
If the Governor decides to withhold assent, he must mandatorily follow the first proviso to Article 200 and return the bill to the Legislature 'as soon as possible' with a message.
The Governor cannot simply declare that he is 'withholding assent' and keep the bill in permanent limbo without returning it to the House.
If the State Legislature passes the bill again, with or without amendment, the Governor is constitutionally bound to grant assent.
The Governor cannot question the validity of an Assembly session reconvened by the Speaker under constitutional assembly rules.
Constitutional functionaries cannot abuse constitutional silence to subvert the democratic will of the elected representatives.

provisions.title: Assent to Bills by Governor
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to bar indefinite pocket vetoes and mandate prompt return of bills to the legislature.

provisions.title: Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor
provisions.relevance: Reaffirmed that the Governor must act on aid and advice in the parliamentary constitutional scheme.

provisions.title: Sessions of the State Legislature, prorogation and dissolution
provisions.relevance: Speaker's authority to adjourn and reconvene assembly sittings upheld against Governor's interference.

54.overview: The State of Punjab enacted the Punjab Scheduled Castes and Backward Classes (Reservation in Services) Act, 2006, creating a 50% preferential sub-quota within Scheduled Caste reservations for Valmikis and Mazhabi Sikhs. A 7-judge Constitution Bench was constituted to reconsider the 5-judge bench decision in E.V. Chinnaiah (2004), which had held that Scheduled Castes form a single homogeneous class incapable of sub-division.
54.issues: Whether State Governments have the legislative competence under Articles 15(4), 16(4), and 341 to sub-classify Scheduled Castes for affirmative action, and whether E.V. Chinnaiah laid down correct law.
54.holding: A 7-judge Constitution Bench (6:1 majority) overruled E.V. Chinnaiah and held that State Governments have the constitutional power to create sub-classifications within Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to extend preferential benefits to more disadvantaged groups, subject to empirical data and the exclusion of the creamy layer.
key_findings: Scheduled Castes are not a single homogeneous, indivisible class; deep inequalities and differing levels of social and educational backwardness exist within the group.
Sub-classification does not amount to tampering with the Presidential List under Article 341; it merely identifies priority beneficiaries within the recognized list.
Substantive equality under Article 14 and Article 16(4) demands differential treatment for unequal groups within backward classes to prevent reservation benefits from being monopolized.
The State's power to sub-classify must be based on objective, verifiable, and quantifiable empirical data demonstrating inadequate representation of the sub-group.
The State cannot allocate 100% of the reservation quota to a single sub-group or completely exclude any caste in the Presidential List from consideration.
A majority of the judges on the Bench held that the 'creamy layer' principle applies to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to ensure affirmative action reaches the truly downtrodden.
E.V. Chinnaiah was overruled as taking an overly formalistic and rigid approach contrary to substantive equality.

provisions.title: Scheduled Castes Presidential notification
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to allow states to calibrate reservation benefits without altering the notified caste list.

provisions.title: Reservation in public employment
provisions.relevance: Applied under substantive equality to permit targeted sub-quotas for extremely marginalized sub-castes.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Held to justify differential treatment among unequals to prevent elite capture of reservation benefits.

55.overview: The appellant, Romesh Sharma, was chargesheeted in complex criminal proceedings involving extortion and cheating. The Special Judge framed charges, and the High Court declined to interfere. The appellant approached the Supreme Court challenging the order framing charges under Section 228 CrPC on the ground that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case.
55.issues: What is the standard of judicial scrutiny at the stage of framing charges under Sections 227 and 228 of the CrPC, and whether trial courts can weigh evidentiary probity as if conducting a final trial.
55.holding: The Supreme Court held that at the stage of framing charges, the court is not required to conduct a roving inquiry or weigh evidence beyond reasonable doubt. If there is a strong suspicion founded on material that leads the court to form a presumptive opinion of guilt, charge must be framed.
key_findings: At the stage of Sections 227 and 228 CrPC, the court is concerned with whether there is ground for presuming that the accused has committed an offence.
The court must evaluate the material on record produced by the prosecution to ascertain whether the essential ingredients of the alleged offence are prima facie disclosed.
The trial judge cannot evaluate whether the evidence is sufficient for conviction or weigh the defence evidence at the preliminary charge-framing stage.
A roving inquiry or mini-trial is strictly impermissible when deciding discharge applications under Section 227 CrPC.
If two views are equally possible from the material, the view supporting the prosecution's charge is adopted for proceeding to trial.
Strong suspicion founded on material before the court is adequate to frame a charge under Section 228 CrPC.
Appellate and revisional courts should exercise great caution before interdicting trial proceedings at the charge-framing stage.

provisions.title: Discharge in sessions trial
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to establish that discharge is permissible only when allegations are completely groundless.

provisions.title: Framing of charge
provisions.relevance: Authoritative standard of 'grave suspicion' and prima facie case defined.

provisions.title: Discharge and framing of charge
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision in the new procedural code embodying the prima facie standard.

56.overview: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda was convicted of murdering his newly married wife, Manju, by administering potassium cyanide poison. The case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, consisting of alleged marital discord, recovery of chemical substances, and letters written by the deceased. The High Court confirmed the death sentence, leading to an appeal before the Supreme Court.
56.issues: What principles govern conviction based entirely on circumstantial evidence in criminal jurisprudence, and whether the prosecution established an unbroken chain of circumstances excluding every hypothesis of innocence.
56.holding: A 3-judge Bench acquitted the appellant of murder, propounding the immortal 'Panchsheel' (Five Golden Principles) governing circumstantial evidence. The Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove an unbroken chain of circumstances and that suicide could not be ruled out.
key_findings: Condition 1: The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established and proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Condition 2: The facts so established must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and must explain no other hypothesis.
Condition 3: The circumstances must be of a conclusive nature and tendency, pointing unmistakably towards guilt.
Condition 4: The circumstances must exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved (guilt of the accused).
Condition 5: There must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with innocence.
There is a long distance between 'may be true' and 'must be true'; prosecution evidence must bridge that distance through cogent proof.
Graver the crime, higher the standard of proof; emotional outrage or suspicion cannot take the place of legal proof in capital trials.

provisions.title: Interpretation clause - 'Proved'
provisions.relevance: Foundational provision defining the rigorous standard of proof required for circumstantial evidence.

provisions.title: Murder
provisions.relevance: Conviction and death sentence set aside due to broken chain of circumstantial evidence.

provisions.title: Burden of proof
provisions.relevance: Reaffirmed that the burden never shifts to the accused to prove innocence in circumstantial cases.

57.overview: Kishore Singh and other prison inmates in Rajasthan addressed letters to the Supreme Court complaining of brutal third-degree torture, continuous handcuffing, and iron fetters imposed by jail authorities. The Supreme Court took suo motu cognizance to examine state brutality and inhuman conditions in Indian prisons.
57.issues: Whether third-degree torture, arbitrary solitary confinement, and cruel physical restraints in prison violate fundamental human dignity under Article 21, and what is the personal liability of errant police and prison officers.
57.holding: The Supreme Court strongly condemned custodial brutality, holding that human dignity under Article 21 does not vanish behind iron bars. The Court directed state authorities to enforce humane prison standards and held offending police and jail officers personally liable.
key_findings: Third-degree torture, physical beatings, and psychic harassment by law enforcement officers constitute barbaric violations of Article 21.
The State cannot treat convicts or undertrial prisoners as animals devoid of fundamental rights and human dignity.
Police personnel who commit acts of custodial violence cannot claim statutory immunity under state police acts; they are personally answerable to the law.
Prison administrators must treat rehabilitation and human dignity as core goals of penal incarceration.
Subjection of prisoners to iron bar fetters without judicial order is inherently unconstitutional and sadistic.
Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer observed that state torture represents 'constitutional treason' committed against the people.
High Courts were directed to establish prison visitor boards and legal aid clinics to provide immediate avenues of complaint.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to prohibit third-degree torture and inhuman treatment of prisoners.

provisions.title: Prison governance provisions
provisions.relevance: Constrained to prevent sadistic imposition of physical restraints without judicial scrutiny.

58.overview: Prem Shankar Shukla, an undertrial prisoner incarcerated in Tihar Jail, challenged the routine practice of police officers handcuffing him whenever he was escorted to and from the magistrate's court, despite the magistrate having expressly directed that handcuffs should not be used.
58.issues: Whether the routine and mechanical handcuffing of prisoners during escort violates Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
58.holding: A 3-judge Bench held that routine handcuffing of prisoners is prima facie inhuman, degrading, and violative of Articles 14, 19, and 21. Handcuffs can be used only in rare, exceptional cases of violent propensity with prior judicial permission.
key_findings: Handcuffing is prima facie degrading, humiliating, and destructive of human dignity; to bind a human being in chains without justification violates Article 21.
Routine handcuffing is arbitrary and violates equality under Article 14; differentiation based on social status (e.g., class classification for handcuffs) is unconstitutional.
Handcuffs can be used only in extraordinary situations where the prisoner has a demonstrable propensity to violence or grave danger of escape.
Even in exceptional situations, the escorting officer must record reasons in writing and obtain contemporaneous permission from the Magistrate.
The Judicial Magistrate has a positive duty to inspect escorted prisoners and question why any prisoner appears in chains without court order.
Police guidelines and prison manuals permitting routine handcuffing without judicial authorization were declared ultra vires.
Justice Krishna Iyer declared: 'Insurance against escape does not mean licence for barbarity. Human dignity is the hallmark of our constitutional scheme.'

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Enforced to hold that personal dignity prohibits mechanical handcuffing of accused persons.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied to strike down colonial prison rules prescribing different handcuffing rules based on social class.

provisions.title: Use of handcuffs
provisions.relevance: Modern procedural provision regulating when handcuffs may be applied during arrest and escort.

59.overview: Former Chief Minister of Orissa, Nandini Satpathy, was summoned by the Deputy Superintendent of Police (Vigilance) for questioning in a corruption probe under Section 161 CrPC. She refused to answer a long list of written questions, claiming that answering them would expose her to criminal prosecution. She was prosecuted under Section 179 IPC for refusing to answer a public servant.
59.issues: Whether the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and Section 161(2) CrPC applies during police investigation to witnesses and suspects, and whether an accused has the right to remain silent.
59.holding: A 3-judge Bench held that the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) applies not only at the trial stage, but fully extends to the police investigation and questioning stage under Section 161 CrPC. An accused or suspect has the constitutional right to remain silent when questions have a tendency to expose them to a criminal charge.
key_findings: The protection of Article 20(3) is available from the moment a person is questioned as an accused or potential accused by the police.
The phrase 'compelled to be a witness against himself' includes oral and written statements extracted during custodial interrogation.
Section 161(2) CrPC creates a statutory shield: an examined person is bound to answer questions truly, except those having a tendency to expose them to a criminal charge.
Compulsion is not limited to physical torture; subtle psychological pressure, protracted interrogation, and threatening prosecutorial postures constitute prohibited compulsion.
The suspect is entitled to silence when a question has a tendency to incriminate, and silence cannot be punished as an offence under Section 179 IPC.
The prosecution of Nandini Satpathy under Section 179 IPC was quashed as unconstitutional.
The Court recommended that an accused should be allowed the presence of their legal counsel within viewing distance during police interrogation.

provisions.title: Right against self-incrimination
provisions.relevance: Authoritatively extended to pre-trial police interrogation under Section 161 CrPC.

provisions.title: Examination of witnesses by police - Right against self-incrimination
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to create a complete statutory right to remain silent against incriminatory questions.

provisions.title: Refusing to answer public servant authorized to question
provisions.relevance: Held inapplicable where the refusal is based on the constitutional exercise of the right to silence.

60.overview: In the infamous Bhagalpur Blinding incident in Bihar, police personnel deliberately blinded over 30 undertrial prisoners by puncturing their eyes with needles and pouring acid (gangajali) into them. A PIL was filed under Article 32 by advocate Kapil Sibal and activist groups seeking medical relief, rehabilitation, and compensation for the blinded victims.
60.issues: Whether police brutality resulting in horrific physical mutilation violates Article 21, and whether the Supreme Court has the power under Article 32 to grant monetary compensation to victims of state atrocities.
60.holding: The Supreme Court held that the barbaric blindings committed by police officers constituted an abhorrent violation of Article 21. The Court ordered the State to provide specialized medical treatment at state expense and affirmed that monetary compensation must be awarded for state-sponsored human rights violations.
key_findings: Deliberate infliction of blindness and physical mutilation on undertrial prisoners is a horrific crime that shocks the conscience of humanity.
The State cannot escape responsibility for the barbaric acts committed by its police officers while discharging official functions.
Under Article 21, the right to life includes the right to bodily integrity and freedom from torture, which cannot be denied even to alleged criminals.
The Court ordered that all blinded prisoners be brought to the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, for specialized treatment at state expense.
The State of Bihar was directed to provide immediate monetary sustenance and lifelong pensions to the victims and their families.
The Court directed criminal prosecution of all police officers involved in the blinding atrocities.
This decision helped pioneer the doctrine of 'Public Law Damages' and state liability for constitutional torts in India.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Bedrock provision applied to condemn police atrocities and establish state duty of medical rehabilitation.

provisions.title: Remedies for enforcement of fundamental rights
provisions.relevance: Enforced to grant interim monetary compensation and medical assistance directly from the bench.

61.overview: Journalist and social activist Sheela Barse addressed a letter to the Supreme Court complaining of custodial violence, sexual harassment, and illegal confinement of women prisoners in police lockups in the City of Bombay.
61.issues: What safeguards must be established to protect female prisoners in police custody from torture, sexual harassment, and arbitrary detention under Articles 21 and 22.
61.holding: The Supreme Court treated the letter as a writ petition and issued mandatory directives to protect female prisoners, including separate lockups, female police escorts, immediate legal aid, and judicial inspections.
key_findings: Women prisoners in police lockups are extraordinarily vulnerable to physical, custodial, and sexual abuse by male law enforcement officers.
Female prisoners must be detained in separate lockups guarded exclusively by female police constables.
Interrogation of women suspects must be conducted strictly in the presence of female police personnel.
Immediately upon arrest, the arresting officer must inform the arrested woman of the grounds of arrest and provide access to free legal aid.
The police must inform the nearest Legal Aid Committee immediately upon arresting any indigent female prisoner.
Magistrates must inspect police lockups in their jurisdiction periodically without prior notice to verify conditions.
Any custodial violence or abuse reported by a female prisoner must be investigated immediately with mandatory medical examination.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Enforced to mandate humane, safe, and dignified custodial treatment for female arrestees.

provisions.title: Equal justice and free legal aid
provisions.relevance: Mandated immediate notification of legal aid committees upon arrest of women suspects.

provisions.title: Arrest of woman
provisions.relevance: Legislative reform later enacted restricting night-time arrests of women pursuant to these judicial guidelines.

62.overview: Rudal Sah was acquitted by a Sessions Court in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, in 1968, but despite his acquittal, he was illegally detained in jail for over 14 years until a habeas corpus petition was moved in 1982. The State admitted the illegal detention as an administrative error, prompting the Court to consider whether mere release was an adequate remedy.
62.issues: Whether mere release of an illegally detained citizen is sufficient, or whether the Supreme Court has the power under Article 32 to award monetary compensation for the violation of fundamental rights under Article 21.
62.holding: The Supreme Court held that the state's illegal detention of Rudal Sah for 14 years violated Article 21. The Court ordered the State of Bihar to pay monetary compensation of Rs 35,000 as interim compensation, establishing the historic doctrine of 'Constitutional Tort'.
key_findings: Illegal detention of an acquitted citizen for 14 years constitutes an outrageous and egregious violation of Article 21.
Article 32 is not confined to issuing traditional writs of habeas corpus; the Court has the power to forge new remedies, including monetary compensation.
To relegate an impoverished victim of state lawlessness to a protracted civil suit for damages would be a mockery of justice and constitutional guarantees.
The State must be held liable for compensatory damages when its functionaries violate fundamental rights through gross negligence or mala fides.
Monetary compensation in public law is awarded to serve as a palliative measure for unlawful deprivation of liberty and a deterrent against state apathy.
The award of compensation under Article 32 does not bar the victim from pursuing further common law damages in a civil suit.
This decision laid the foundational cornerstone for the doctrine of constitutional tort in Indian administrative and human rights jurisprudence.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Directly violated by 14 years of unlawful post-acquittal incarceration.

provisions.title: Remedies for enforcement of fundamental rights
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to authorize the award of monetary compensation for gross violations of fundamental rights.

63.overview: Suman Behera, a 22-year-old youth, was picked up by the police in Orissa for interrogation in a theft case and died in police custody. His body was found tied with rope on a railway track. His mother, Nilabati Behera, addressed a letter to the Supreme Court seeking justice and compensation for the custodial killing of her son.
63.issues: Whether the defence of sovereign immunity applies to violations of fundamental rights under Article 21, and what are the principles governing public law compensation for custodial deaths under Article 32.
63.holding: The Supreme Court held that the death was a custodial homicide by police personnel, violating Article 21. The Court rejected the defence of sovereign immunity, ruled that public law compensation is distinct from private law damages, and ordered the State of Orissa to pay Rs 1,50,000 compensation.
key_findings: Custodial death is one of the worst crimes in a civilized society governed by the rule of law.
Prisoners and detainees do not lose their fundamental right to life; the State owes a strict duty of care to ensure the safety and survival of persons in custody.
The defence of sovereign immunity (enunciated in Kasturi Lal) has no application to proceedings for enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 32 or Article 226.
Public law compensation for violation of fundamental rights is a constitutional remedy based on strict liability, entirely distinct from private law tort claims.
The purpose of public law compensation is to provide immediate succour to victims of state violence and enforce the accountability of state authorities.
When a person dies in police custody, the burden rests squarely on the police to explain how the injuries were sustained.
The State of Orissa was granted liberty to recover the compensation amount from the individual police officers responsible for the custodial murder.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Formulated as an inviolable guarantee placing strict custodial safety liability on the State.

provisions.title: Remedies for enforcement of fundamental rights
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as empowering the Court to award public law compensation free from sovereign immunity defences.

64.overview: Chaudhary Bhajan Lal, former Chief Minister of Haryana, challenged an FIR registered against him under the Prevention of Corruption Act alleging accumulation of disproportionate assets. The High Court of Punjab & Haryana quashed the FIR and the investigation, prompting the State of Haryana to appeal to the Supreme Court.
64.issues: What are the parameters and guidelines governing the High Court's extraordinary power under Article 226 and inherent powers under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash an FIR and criminal investigation at the inception.
64.holding: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's quashing order and permitted the investigation to proceed. The Court laid down the famous seven illustrative categories of cases where High Courts can exercise their inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash an FIR.
key_findings: Category 1: Where allegations in the FIR, taken at their face value, do not prima facie constitute any offence.
Category 2: Where allegations are so absurd and inherently improbable that no prudent person can reach a conclusion of ground for proceeding.
Category 3: Where criminal proceedings are manifestly attended with mala fides or maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for vengeance.
Category 4: Where there is an express legal bar under the CrPC or concerned statute to the institution and continuance of the proceedings.
Category 5: Where uncontroverted allegations in the FIR do not disclose the commission of any cognizable offence justifying police investigation.
Category 6: Where evidence collected does not disclose a cognizable offence, but only a non-cognizable offence without Magistrate sanction.
Category 7: The power of quashing is an extraordinary power that must be exercised with extreme caution and circumspection; courts cannot stifle legitimate police investigation into corruption.

provisions.title: Saving of inherent powers of High Court
provisions.relevance: Foundational provision under which the seven landmark guidelines for quashing criminal proceedings were formulated.

provisions.title: Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
provisions.relevance: Harmonized with Section 482 CrPC for reviewing criminal proceedings at the threshold stage.

provisions.title: Inherent powers of High Court
provisions.relevance: The corresponding provision in the new procedural code embodying the Bhajan Lal quashing matrix.

65.overview: Deoman Upadhyaya was convicted of murdering his stepmother with a gandasa. In police custody, he stated 'I had thrown the gandasa into the tank, I will take it out and give it to you', leading to the discovery of the bloodstained weapon. The High Court acquitted him, holding that Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act discriminated between persons in custody and persons not in custody, violating Article 14.
65.issues: Whether Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, which permits the admission of confessions leading to the discovery of facts by persons in police custody, violates the guarantee of equality under Article 14.
65.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act is constitutionally valid and does not violate Article 14. The Court upheld the conviction, ruling that the classification between persons in custody and persons not in custody is reasonable and based on intelligible differentia.
key_findings: Section 27 operates as a qualified proviso to the blanket ban on confessions made to police officers under Sections 25 and 26 of the Evidence Act.
The rationale behind Section 27 is the doctrine of confirmation by subsequent facts; when a tangible fact is discovered pursuant to a statement, the risk of fabrication is eliminated.
The classification between persons in police custody and persons not in custody is founded on intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object of investigation.
Section 27 does not violate Article 14 because all persons placed in police custody are treated equally and subject to the same evidentiary rule.
Only so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered is admissible in evidence; the confession of guilt remains excluded.
The discovery of the weapon of assault from a hidden location solely within the accused's knowledge constitutes powerful corroborative evidence.
Justice Subba Rao delivered a notable dissent, arguing that Section 27 creates an irrational differential between custody and non-custody confessions.

provisions.title: How much of information received from accused may be proved
provisions.relevance: Constitutional validity upheld under Article 14 as a valid exception to the confession ban.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied through reasonable classification doctrine to sustain the custody-based evidentiary provision.

provisions.title: Discovery of facts pursuant to information
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision under the BSA codifying Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act.

66.overview: In a murder case from Madras, the accused, Pulukuri Kottaya and others, made a statement to the police: 'About 14 days ago, I, Kotayya and others beat Chinna Kotayya and Vanya to death. I hid the spear and stick in the rick in the village. I will show you the place and produce them.' The trial court admitted the entire statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
66.issues: What is the true scope and construction of Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, and whether a confession of guilt can be admitted along with the statement leading to the discovery of an object.
66.holding: The Privy Council, speaking through Sir John Beaumont, laid down the classic and definitive interpretation of Section 27. The Court held that only that part of the statement which distinctly relates to the discovery of the physical fact (the hiding place) is admissible; the confession of having beaten the deceased to death is inadmissible.
key_findings: Section 27 of the Evidence Act is an exception to Sections 25 and 26 and must be construed strictly to prevent police circumvention of the confession ban.
The expression 'fact discovered' in Section 27 does not mean the physical object alone; it embraces the place from which the object is produced and the knowledge of the accused as to this.
The information admitted must relate distinctly to that discovery; 'distinctly' means directly, unequivocally, and strictly.
A statement by the accused that he committed the murder or beat the deceased does not relate distinctly to the discovery of the spear or stick and must be severed and excluded.
The admissible portion is strictly limited to: 'I hid the spear in the rick; I will show you the place and produce it.'
Trial courts and prosecutors cannot smuggle confessions of past guilt into evidence under the guise of Section 27 recovery memos.
This decision remains the bedrock of discovery evidence across the Indian subcontinent for over seven decades.

provisions.title: Information received from accused leading to discovery
provisions.relevance: Authoritative interpretation separating the admissible discovery statement from the inadmissible confession.

provisions.title: Confession to police officer not to be proved
provisions.relevance: Protected from dilution by enforcing the strict severance test under Section 27.

provisions.title: Discovery of facts
provisions.relevance: The new evidence code continues the foundational Pulukuri Kottaya severance doctrine.

67.overview: Pakala Narayana Swami was tried and convicted for the murder of Kurunathan, whose dismembered body was found in a steel trunk in a train compartment at Puri. The prosecution relied heavily on a statement made by the deceased to his wife that he was going to Berhampur to collect money from the accused, as well as an alleged statement made by the accused to the police.
67.issues: Whether the deceased's statement to his wife was admissible as a dying declaration under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act, and what constitutes a 'confession' under Indian evidence law.
67.holding: The Privy Council, speaking through Lord Atkin, upheld the conviction, establishing the classic definition of a 'confession' and the scope of dying declarations under Section 32(1). The Court held that statements relating to the circumstances of the transaction that resulted in death are admissible.
key_findings: A confession must either admit in terms the offence, or at any rate substantially all the facts which constitute the offence.
An admission of an incriminating fact, howsoever grave, is not in itself a confession; a statement that contains self-exculpatory matter cannot be parsed into a confession.
Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act is wider than the English law of dying declarations; the declarant need not be under expectation of death when making the statement.
The phrase 'circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death' includes statements concerning the cause of death or proximate transactions leading up to the death.
The statement of the deceased that he was going to the accused's house to collect debts was directly connected with the transaction resulting in his murder and was fully admissible.
Circumstantial evidence consisting of purchase of the steel trunk, hiring of a cart, and recovery of bloodstains created an unbroken chain establishing guilt.
Lord Atkin's formulation remains the universal definition of confession applied across common law jurisdictions in India.

provisions.title: Statements relating to cause of death (Dying Declaration)
provisions.relevance: Classic interpretation holding that expectation of death is not required and circumstances of transaction are admissible.

provisions.title: Admissions and Confessions
provisions.relevance: Formulated the foundational legal distinction between an admission and a confession.

provisions.title: Statements by persons who cannot be called as witnesses
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision in the BSA continuing the Pakala Narayana Swami doctrine.

68.overview: Kashmira Singh was tried and convicted of the murder of a child, Ramesh, along with co-accused Gurudayal Singh. The Sessions Court and High Court based the conviction almost exclusively on the confession made by the co-accused Gurudayal Singh under Section 30 of the Evidence Act, corroborated by circumstantial recoveries.
68.issues: What is the evidentiary value of a confession of a co-accused under Section 30 of the Indian Evidence Act, and whether a conviction can be sustained primarily on such a confession.
68.holding: The Supreme Court acquitted Kashmira Singh, holding that a co-accused's confession under Section 30 is not substantive evidence against other accused. It can only be used as supportive material to 'lend assurance' to other independent evidence, and cannot form the foundation of a conviction.
key_findings: The confession of a co-accused is not 'evidence' as defined in Section 3 of the Evidence Act because it is not given on oath and not tested by cross-examination.
Section 30 merely permits the Court to 'take into consideration' such confession against other persons being tried jointly for the same offence.
A court cannot begin its assessment with the co-accused's confession; it must first evaluate the independent evidence marshaled against the accused.
If the independent evidence is strong and points towards guilt, the co-accused's confession may be used only to lend assurance to the court's conclusion.
A co-accused's confession cannot be made the foundation of a conviction or used to bridge gaps in weak prosecution evidence.
The testimony of an accomplice stands on a higher footing than a co-accused confession, but even accomplice testimony requires independent corroboration under Section 114 Illustration (b).
Since the independent evidence against Kashmira Singh was insufficient, the co-accused's confession could not rescue the prosecution case.

provisions.title: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial
provisions.relevance: Authoritatively established that co-accused confessions are not substantive evidence and can only lend assurance.

provisions.title: Court may presume existence of certain facts - Accomplice testimony
provisions.relevance: Applied to require independent corroborative evidence in material particulars.

provisions.title: Consideration of proved confession affecting co-accused
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision under the BSA maintaining the supportive-only evidentiary threshold.

69.overview: In a horrifying child sacrifice murder case in Maharashtra, two minor children were murdered. The prosecution relied on the recovery of human skeletal remains and bicycles based on information provided by the accused under Section 27 Evidence Act, as well as expert opinion identifying the bicycles from tyre impressions under Section 45.
69.issues: What constitutes the 'fact discovered' under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and whether expert evidence regarding tyre impressions and recovery of dead bodies can sustain a conviction.
69.holding: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction, clarifying the evidentiary mechanism of Section 27. The Court held that the recovery of the bodies from a secluded spot solely known to the accused constituted discovery of fact, and tyre impression evidence under Section 45 was reliable corroboration.
key_findings: The basic idea embedded in Section 27 Evidence Act is the doctrine of confirmation by subsequent events.
The 'fact discovered' is not just the physical article recovered, but the mental knowledge of the accused that the article was concealed at that particular spot.
Recovery of bodies or incriminating articles from places open and accessible to the general public cannot be accepted as discovery solely within the knowledge of the accused.
However, if the article is concealed or hidden from public view in a secluded spot, the discovery statement is fully admissible under Section 27.
Opinion of an expert under Section 45 regarding tyre mark impressions, footprints, and forensic matching is admissible as supportive scientific evidence.
When recoveries are made in quick succession based on voluntary disclosure, the inference of complicity becomes irresistible.
Reaffirmed the principle that reliable circumstantial recoveries provide strong corroboration to establish criminal guilt.

provisions.title: Information received from accused leading to discovery
provisions.relevance: Applied to admit recovery of concealed skeletal remains from secluded spots.

provisions.title: Opinions of experts
provisions.relevance: Applied to validate forensic analysis of tyre impressions and physical marks.

provisions.title: Opinions of experts
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision in the new BSA continuing expert opinion admissibility.

70.overview: The appellant was tried for murder and acquitted by the trial court. The High Court reversed the acquittal on appeal and convicted him under Section 302 IPC. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, contending that the appellate court had disregarded the settled principles governing interference with an order of acquittal.
70.issues: What are the powers of an appellate court in dealing with an order of acquittal under Section 378 CrPC, and what is the strength of the presumption of innocence in criminal trials.
70.holding: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the acquittal. The Court reiterated that the presumption of innocence is reinforced by an order of acquittal, and appellate courts should interfere only when trial court findings are manifestly perverse or wholly unsustainable.
key_findings: The presumption of innocence is a human right and the foundational golden thread running through criminal jurisprudence.
When the trial court acquits an accused, the initial presumption of innocence is not weakened; rather, it is doubled and reinforced.
An appellate court undoubtedly has full power under Section 378 CrPC to review, re-appreciate, and reconsider the entire evidence.
However, the appellate court should not reverse an acquittal merely because a second view on the evidence is possible.
If two reasonable views are possible on the evidence, the view adopted by the trial court that favours the accused must be preferred.
Interference with an acquittal is warranted only where the trial court's judgment is perverse, palpably erroneous, or based on gross misreading of evidence.
The High Court erred in substituting its subjective view for the plausible and well-reasoned view of the Sessions Judge.

provisions.title: Appeal in case of acquittal
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to strictly constrain appellate interference with plausible acquittal verdicts.

provisions.title: Powers of the Appellate Court
provisions.relevance: Exercised to restore trial court acquittal where reversal was ungrounded in perversity.

provisions.title: Appeals against acquittal
provisions.relevance: Corresponding BNSS provision governing high standards for reversing acquittal.

71.overview: In a double murder case, the primary eyewitness was a deaf and mute woman who communicated through signs and gestures, along with a child witness. The trial court and High Court convicted the accused. In appeal before the Supreme Court, the defence challenged the competence and admissibility of a speech-impaired witness under Section 119 of the Evidence Act.
71.issues: Whether a dumb or speech-impaired witness is competent to testify under Section 119 of the Evidence Act, and what safeguards must be observed when recording evidence through signs and gestures.
71.holding: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction, holding that a dumb or speech-impaired witness is fully competent to give evidence under Section 119 of the Evidence Act. Evidence recorded through signs in open court is deemed to be oral evidence in law.
key_findings: Section 119 of the Evidence Act enables any witness who is unable to speak to give evidence in any manner in which they can make it intelligible, including signs.
Evidence given by a speech-impaired witness by signs in open court is deemed to be oral evidence under Section 119.
The court must take special care to ensure that the witness understands the questions and that the signs are accurately recorded, if necessary with the assistance of a trained interpreter.
A deaf and mute witness is not incompetent; to deny them the opportunity to testify would leave victims of crime without voice and justice.
The testimony of child witnesses must be scrutinized with care to rule out tutoring, but if consistent and natural, it forms a reliable basis for conviction.
The evidence of the speech-impaired eyewitness in this case was natural, consistent, and fully corroborated by medical and forensic recoveries.
Section 119 was amended legislatively in 2013 to mandatorily require video recording of statements of speech-impaired witnesses.

provisions.title: Witness unable to communicate verbally (Dumb witness)
provisions.relevance: Directly applied to validate evidence recorded by signs and gestures as admissible oral evidence.

provisions.title: Who may testify
provisions.relevance: Affirmed broad witness competence subject only to understanding questions and giving rational answers.

provisions.title: Witness unable to communicate verbally
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision under the BSA maintaining witness accessibility.

72.overview: In a kidnapping and murder trial in Bihar, the prosecution had no direct eyewitnesses and relied upon an extra-judicial confession allegedly made by the accused to a village mukhiya, combined with circumstantial evidence and recovery of the victim's bicycle.
72.issues: What is the evidentiary value of an extra-judicial confession in criminal trials, and whether conviction can be founded on an uncorroborated extra-judicial confession.
72.holding: The Supreme Court acquitted the appellant, holding that an extra-judicial confession is inherently a weak piece of evidence. It can be relied upon only if voluntary, consistent, and corroborated by independent cogent evidence.
key_findings: An extra-judicial confession is by nature a weak piece of evidence; it must be received with great caution and circumspection by courts.
Before accepting an extra-judicial confession, the court must ascertain the exact words spoken, the person to whom it was made, and whether the confession was voluntary.
If the person to whom the confession was made had no authority, no close relationship, or no reason for the accused to confide in them, the confession becomes suspect.
An uncorroborated extra-judicial confession cannot form the sole basis of conviction in a serious criminal trial.
Circumstantial evidence must satisfy the test of an unbroken chain; recovery of a common bicycle without distinct identification marks is insufficient to establish murder.
Where the prosecution fails to establish that the confession was natural and spontaneous, it must be excluded from consideration.
Reiterated that suspicion, however grave, cannot substitute for legal proof beyond reasonable doubt.

provisions.title: Confession caused by inducement, threat or promise
provisions.relevance: Applied to test the voluntariness and credibility of extra-judicial confessions.

provisions.title: Murder
provisions.relevance: Conviction set aside due to unreliable extra-judicial confession and broken circumstantial chain.

73.overview: In the sensational Jain Hawala case, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) chargesheeted senior politicians, including V.C. Shukla and L.K. Advani, under the Prevention of Corruption Act based on loose spiral notebooks and diary entries seized from the Jain brothers containing initials and alleged pay-off amounts.
73.issues: Whether loose sheets, spiral diaries, and files constitute 'books of account regularly kept in the course of business' under Section 34 of the Indian Evidence Act, and whether entries in such diaries can create criminal liability without independent corroborative evidence.
73.holding: The Supreme Court discharged the accused, holding that loose sheets of paper bound in a spiral notebook do not constitute 'books of account regularly kept in the course of business' under Section 34 Evidence Act. Furthermore, entries in books of account alone cannot create liability without independent evidence of payment.
key_findings: To qualify as a 'book of account' under Section 34 Evidence Act, there must be a collection of sheets permanently bound together at the time of entry, showing continuity of transactions.
Loose sheets of paper, spiral pads, and unbound files do not satisfy the statutory definition of 'books of account'.
The requirement that books must be 'regularly kept in the course of business' implies that entries are made contemporaneously in the ordinary routine of business operations.
Section 34 explicitly enacts that entries in books of account, though admissible, 'shall not alone be sufficient evidence to charge any person with liability'.
There must be independent, extraneous evidence showing the actual receipt of the money or the underlying transaction to create criminal or civil liability.
Cryptic initials and figures in a private diary cannot form the basis of a criminal chargesheet against named public figures without corroboration.
The High Court's order discharging the respondents under Section 227 CrPC was upheld.

provisions.title: Entries in books of account, including those maintained in an electronic form, when relevant
provisions.relevance: Authoritatively interpreted to exclude loose sheets and prohibit liability based solely on diary entries.

provisions.title: Sections 7 & 13
provisions.relevance: Corruption charges dropped due to lack of admissible primary accounting proof of illicit gratification.

provisions.title: Entries in books of account
provisions.relevance: Corresponding provision under the BSA maintaining the mandatory corroboration rule.

74.overview: The Chief Commissioner of Delhi issued an order under Section 7(1)(c) of the East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949 imposing pre-censorship on Brij Bhushan, printer and publisher of the English weekly journal 'Organizer'. The order directed the editor to submit all communal matter and Pakistan-related news to the state censor prior to publication.
74.issues: Whether the imposition of pre-censorship on a newspaper violates the fundamental freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a).
74.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down the pre-censorship order and Section 7(1)(c) of the Act, holding that pre-censorship is a gross violation of freedom of the press and the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
key_findings: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes the freedom of the press, which is the cornerstone of democratic governance.
Imposition of pre-censorship on a journal is a serious restriction on the liberty of the press and cannot be tolerated under the Constitution.
Prior restraint and pre-censorship are inherently inimical to free public discussion and political criticism.
The original grounds of restriction under Article 19(2) were limited to security of the State and did not include public order or public safety.
A statute permitting executive pre-censorship on vague grounds of public safety is unconstitutional in its entirety.
Justice Fazl Ali dissented, maintaining that communal publications during partition justified preventive administrative oversight.
This decision, along with Romesh Thappar, prompted Parliament to enact the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951, introducing 'public order' into Article 19(2).

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression (Freedom of the Press)
