provisions.relevance: Applied to strike down executive pre-censorship of newspapers as fundamentally unconstitutional.

provisions.title: Reasonable restrictions on speech
provisions.relevance: Strictly interpreted to exclude general public safety as a valid ground for press censorship.

provisions.title: Section 7(1)(c)
provisions.relevance: Pre-censorship authorization held unconstitutional and severed.

75.overview: The Department of Telecommunications invited tenders for granting licenses to operate cellular mobile telephone services in four metropolitan cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai). Unsuccessful bidders, including Tata Cellular, challenged the award of licenses, alleging arbitrary tender criteria and bias in tender evaluation.
75.issues: What is the scope and principles governing judicial review of administrative action in government tenders, public contracts, and commercial decisions under Article 226 and Article 32.
75.holding: The Supreme Court formulated the foundational principles of judicial review in public procurement. The Court held that judicial review is not an appeal against the merits of a commercial decision, but a review of the decision-making process to ensure fairness, transparency, and non-arbitrariness.
key_findings: The modern state is a major commercial player; in awarding public contracts, the government must act fairly, transparently, and without bias or arbitrariness under Article 14.
Judicial review is concerned not with the correctness of the decision itself, but with the decision-making process.
The court does not sit as an appellate authority over government tenders or substitute its business judgment for that of technical experts.
Grounds for judicial review of commercial tenders are: (1) illegality (breach of statutory rule); (2) irrationality / Wednesbury unreasonableness; and (3) procedural impropriety.
The government must be given a reasonable 'free play in the joints' in formulating commercial terms and tender conditions.
The terms of the invitation to tender cannot be open to judicial scrutiny unless they are tailor-made to favour a particular bidder or manifestly arbitrary.
Quashing public contracts should be avoided when public interest and project delivery would be adversely affected by delay.

provisions.title: Equality before law - Non-arbitrariness in state action
provisions.relevance: Enforced as the primary constitutional touchstone governing public contracts and state tenders.

provisions.title: Judicial review of administrative action
provisions.relevance: Defined as a review of the decision-making process rather than a merits appeal over commercial choices.

76.overview: Justice K. Veeraswami, retired Chief Justice of the Madras High Court, was chargesheeted by the CBI under Section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for possessing assets disproportionate to his known sources of income. The appellant challenged the criminal proceedings, contending that High Court and Supreme Court judges are constitutional functionaries and not 'public servants' under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
76.issues: Whether a judge of the High Court or Supreme Court is a 'public servant' within the meaning of the Prevention of Corruption Act, and who is the competent authority to grant sanction for prosecution of a superior court judge under Section 6 of the Act.
76.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that a judge of a High Court or the Supreme Court is a 'public servant' within the meaning of the Prevention of Corruption Act. To protect judicial independence, the Court ruled that no FIR can be registered against a superior court judge without prior consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
key_findings: Superior court judges are public servants within the meaning of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and 1988; no one is above the law.
Judges hold a sacred public office; public confidence in the integrity of the judicial administration is essential to the rule of law.
To prevent vexatious, frivolous, or politically motivated prosecutions against judges, mandatory procedural safeguards were instituted.
No criminal case or FIR can be registered against a sitting High Court or Supreme Court judge without prior consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
If the Chief Justice of India is of opinion that there is no prima facie case or material, no further criminal proceedings can be initiated.
The President of India is the competent authority to grant sanction for the prosecution of a High Court or Supreme Court judge under Section 6 of the Act.
Justice J.S. Verma dissented, holding that the statutory sanction scheme was unworkable for constitutional court judges without constitutional amendment.

provisions.title: Section 2 & 5(1)(e)
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass constitutional court judges within the definition of 'public servant'.

provisions.title: Removal and tenure of judges
provisions.relevance: Harmonized with criminal penal statutes to insulate judges from executive harassment.

provisions.title: Complete justice power
provisions.relevance: Invoked to mandate prior consultation with the Chief Justice of India before registering criminal complaints.

77.overview: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad filed a PIL under Article 32 regarding massive illegal deforestation, timber felling, and encroachment in the tropical rainforests of Gudalur in the Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu. The matter expanded into a pan-India continuing mandamus to halt ecological destruction across Indian forests.
77.issues: What is the legal definition and scope of 'forest' under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, and whether state governments can permit non-forest activities without prior approval of the Central Government.
77.holding: The Supreme Court delivered a landmark ruling expanding the definition of 'forest' to its dictionary meaning, covering all statutorily recognized forests, reserve forests, and forested lands regardless of ownership. The Court imposed a nationwide ban on unauthorized tree felling and established the Central Empowered Committee (CEC).
key_findings: The word 'forest' in the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 must not be confined to areas recorded as forests in revenue records; it must be understood in accordance with its broad dictionary meaning.
The Act applies to all forests irrespective of ownership, classification, or private/public status throughout India.
Prior approval of the Central Government under Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is strictly mandatory before clearing or using any forest land for non-forest purposes.
The Court ordered an immediate nationwide freeze on unregulated felling of trees, timber logging, and sawmill operations in forest zones.
The Court instituted the process of 'continuing mandamus', holding periodic hearings to oversee forest governance and wildlife conservation.
Established the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA) to collect Net Present Value (NPV) from project developers.
Constituted the Central Empowered Committee (CEC) as a permanent watchdog committee to assist the Supreme Court in forest disputes.

provisions.title: Section 2: Restriction on de-reservation of forests
provisions.relevance: Authoritatively expanded to apply to all forested lands according to dictionary meaning across India.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass ecological security and preservation of forest ecosystems for future generations.

provisions.title: Protection of environment and forests
provisions.relevance: Applied as a constitutional imperative requiring judicial intervention against state inaction.

78.overview: Kamal Nath, former Union Minister for Environment and Forests, had commercial interests in Span Motels, a luxury resort in Himachal Pradesh. The motel management diverted the course of the Beas River by bulldozing riverbanks and constructing massive concrete embankments to protect their private cottages from seasonal floods, causing severe ecological degradation.
78.issues: Whether the Public Trust Doctrine applies in India, and whether natural resources like rivers, forests, and seashore lands can be converted into private commercial property.
78.holding: A 2-judge Bench held that the Public Trust Doctrine is part of the law of the land in India. The Court held that the State is the trustee of all natural resources and has a legal duty to protect them for the enjoyment of the general public. The motel lease was cancelled and exemplary damages of Rs 10 lakhs were imposed.
key_findings: The Public Trust Doctrine, derived from ancient Roman law and English common law, is part of the environmental jurisprudence of India under Article 21.
The State holds all natural resources—including rivers, seashores, air, forests, and wetlands—as a trustee for the benefit of the general public.
The State is under a legal duty as trustee to protect natural resources and cannot permit their conversion into private commercial ownership or exploitation.
The diversion of the flow of the River Beas by motel management was ecologically disastrous and directly violated the public trust.
The lease granted by the Himachal Pradesh Government encroaching on riverbed land was quashed and set aside.
The enterprise was held liable under the Polluter Pays Principle to pay the entire cost of restoring the natural ecology of the riverbed.
The Supreme Court imposed exemplary pollution fine/damages of Rs 10 lakhs on Span Motels to serve as a deterrent against environmental vandalism.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass the Public Trust Doctrine protecting natural river ecosystems.

provisions.title: Protection of environment and rivers
provisions.relevance: Applied to enforce the state's fiduciary obligation as trustee of ecological resources.

79.overview: The State of Madhya Pradesh entered into long-term commercial agreements allocating raw sal seeds to selected private industrial extraction units without inviting public tenders or holding open auctions. Competing manufacturers challenged the allotment under Article 32 as arbitrary, discriminatory, and conferring private monopolies at state expense.
79.issues: Whether the state's commercial allocation of forest resources through private negotiation violates Article 14, and what is the scope of the doctrine of 'legitimate expectation' in government contracting.
79.holding: The Supreme Court held that while the State must act fairly and non-arbitrarily under Article 14, long-term industrial allocation policies designed to encourage capital investment in backward regions through private negotiation are permissible if founded on bona fide socio-economic considerations and legitimate expectations.
key_findings: State action in allocating scarce industrial raw materials must be tested on the touchstone of non-arbitrariness under Article 14.
Public auction or tender is the general rule for disposing of state largesse, but it is not an inflexible, universal requirement in every industrial policy.
The State is entitled to negotiate with private industrialists to invite capital-intensive infrastructure into industrially backward tribal areas.
The doctrine of 'legitimate expectation' operates in administrative law to protect parties who have invested massive capital based on state policy assurances.
Courts will not interfere with state economic policy merely because a different economic method or higher short-term revenue might have been achieved.
Judicial review is confined to examining whether the government policy was tainted with mala fides, nepotism, or extraneous commercial considerations.
The allocation of sal seeds in this case was sustained as a rational policy to foster agro-processing industry.

provisions.title: Equality before law - Non-arbitrariness in public largesse
provisions.relevance: Applied to balance competitive bidding rules with legitimate state economic development policies.

provisions.title: Right to practice trade and commerce
provisions.relevance: Harmonized with state regulatory powers over forest produce extraction.

80.overview: The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) filed a PIL under Article 32 seeking constitutional recognition for the transgender community. Transgender persons faced extreme social ostracization, denial of civil rights, harassment by law enforcement, and were forced to identify binary genders (male or female) on all official documentation, passports, and ration cards.
80.issues: Whether transgender persons have the fundamental right to legal recognition of their self-identified gender under Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(a), and 21, and whether they are entitled to affirmative action as a socially and educationally backward class.
80.holding: A 2-judge Bench held that transgender persons have the constitutional right to self-identification of their gender as male, female, or 'third gender' under Articles 14, 19, and 21. The Court directed Central and State Governments to treat transgender persons as socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs) for affirmative action.
key_findings: Gender identity is one of the most fundamental aspects of life, referring to each person's deeply felt internal and individual experience of gender.
Self-determination of gender identity is an integral facet of personal autonomy and human dignity protected under Article 21.
Transgender persons have the legal right to identify their gender identity as male, female, or third gender without requiring medical sex-reassignment surgery (SRS).
Discrimination on grounds of gender identity constitutes discrimination on the ground of 'sex' prohibited under Articles 15(1) and 16(2).
Gender expression through dress, speech, mannerisms, and presentation is protected freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a).
Central and State Governments were directed to treat transgender persons as socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs) and extend reservations in education and public employment.
Governments were directed to establish separate public restrooms, specialized healthcare facilities, and social welfare safety nets for the community.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Enforced to mandate non-discrimination and equal protection for gender non-conforming individuals.

provisions.title: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sex
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass discrimination based on gender identity within the term 'sex'.

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression
provisions.relevance: Protects gender presentation, attire, and personal expression from state censure.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Bedrock guarantee establishing gender self-determination as an inalienable component of human dignity.

81.overview: The Indian Young Lawyers Association challenged Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorization of Entry) Rules, 1965, which prohibited women aged 10 to 50 (menstruating age) from entering the historic Sabarimala temple of Lord Ayyappa. The custom was defended by temple thantris as rooted in the celibate nature (Naishtika Brahmacharya) of the deity.
81.issues: Whether the exclusion of women aged 10 to 50 from Sabarimala temple violates Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution, and whether the custom is protected as an Essential Religious Practice under Article 25 and Article 26.
81.holding: By a 4:1 majority, a 5-judge Constitution Bench held that the exclusion of women aged 10 to 50 from Sabarimala temple is unconstitutional and void. The Court struck down Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Rules, ruling that biological physiological characteristics cannot be made the basis for denying women religious worship.
key_findings: Devotion and the right to pray cannot be subjected to gender discrimination; women have an equal constitutional right under Article 25 to enter public temples.
The exclusion of women based on menstruation is a form of gender stereotyping that treats women as impure, directly violating human dignity under Article 21.
Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules, 1965 was held ultra vires the parent Act and violative of Articles 14 and 15.
Ayyappa devotees do not constitute a separate religious denomination under Article 26, but form part of the broader Hindu religious community.
The exclusion of women was not an Essential Religious Practice (ERP) of the Hindu religion and could not claim immunity from constitutional scrutiny.
Justice D.Y. Chandrachud observed that notions of menstrual impurity are a form of 'untouchability' prohibited under Article 17 of the Constitution.
Justice Indu Malhotra delivered a dissenting opinion, emphasizing that constitutional courts should not interfere with bona fide religious beliefs and practices.

provisions.title: Freedom of conscience and free profession of religion
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as guaranteeing equal religious access to women without gender barriers.

provisions.title: Equality and prohibition of discrimination
provisions.relevance: Applied to strike down physiological discrimination based on biological cycles.

provisions.title: Freedom to manage religious affairs
provisions.relevance: Held not to protect exclusionary practices that violate core individual fundamental rights.

provisions.act: Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules, 1965
provisions.title: Exclusion of women based on custom
provisions.relevance: Struck down as unconstitutional and ultra vires.

82.overview: A reference was made to a 5-judge Constitution Bench to reconsider the landmark ruling in M. Nagaraj (2006). The Union Government and states contended that Nagaraj placed an impossible burden on states by requiring them to collect quantifiable data showing the 'backwardness' of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes before granting reservation in promotions under Article 16(4A).
82.issues: Whether the requirement in M. Nagaraj to collect quantifiable data demonstrating backwardness of SCs and STs is invalid, and whether the 'creamy layer' principle applies to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in promotional quotas.
82.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that the requirement in Nagaraj to collect quantifiable data on the backwardness of SCs and STs was contrary to the 9-judge bench decision in Indra Sawhney and is invalid. However, the Court held that the 'creamy layer' principle applies to SCs and STs for reservation in promotions.
key_findings: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are presumed to be backward under Articles 341 and 342; requiring states to collect empirical data of their backwardness was erroneous.
The ruling in M. Nagaraj was overruled to the narrow extent that it mandated collection of quantifiable data on backwardness for SCs and STs.
However, the state is still required to collect quantifiable data showing the 'inadequacy of representation' of SCs and STs in promotional cadres.
The state must ensure that overall administrative efficiency under Article 335 is maintained while providing promotional quotas.
The 'creamy layer' exclusion principle is an essential facet of the constitutional equality code under Articles 14 and 16(1).
The creamy layer doctrine applies to SCs and STs to prevent individuals who have achieved high socio-economic status from cornering promotional benefits at the expense of disadvantaged brethren.
Exclusion of the creamy layer does not alter or tinker with the Presidential List under Article 341 or Article 342.

provisions.title: Reservation in matters of promotion for SCs and STs
provisions.relevance: Harmonized by removing data-of-backwardness hurdle while applying creamy layer exclusion.

provisions.title: Claims of SCs and STs to services and posts (Efficiency of administration)
provisions.relevance: Applied as an overarching balancing principle during promotional reservations.

provisions.title: Presidential Orders for SCs and STs
provisions.relevance: Presumption of backwardness affirmed as inherent to presidential constitutional notification.

83.overview: A 5-judge Constitution Bench heard the substantive challenge to the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016. Petitioners challenged the mandatory linkage of Aadhaar with bank accounts, SIM cards, school admissions, and income tax PAN cards, as well as the passage of the Act as a Money Bill.
83.issues: Whether the Aadhaar Act, 2016 violates the fundamental right to privacy under Article 21, whether Section 57 permitting private corporate usage is unconstitutional, and whether the Act was validly passed as a Money Bill under Article 110.
83.holding: A 4:1 majority upheld the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar Act, 2016 for government welfare subsidies, but struck down Section 57 permitting private corporate access, severed mandatory linkage with bank accounts and mobile phones, and struck down school admission mandates.
key_findings: The Aadhaar Act fulfills a legitimate state aim of targeted delivery of welfare benefits, subsidies, and socio-economic rights to marginalized citizens.
Section 7 of the Act, which mandates Aadhaar authentication for receiving state-funded subsidies, benefits, and services from the Consolidated Fund of India, is constitutional.
Section 57 of the Act, which allowed private corporations, telecom operators, and banks to demand Aadhaar numbers, was struck down as unconstitutional and violative of privacy.
Mandatory linkage of Aadhaar with mobile SIM cards and bank accounts was declared unconstitutional and disproportionate under Article 21.
Schools and educational boards cannot insist on Aadhaar enrollment for admitting minor children to schools or examinations.
Section 33(2) (disclosure of biometric data on national security grounds) was read down to require judicial oversight by a High Court judge.
Justice D.Y. Chandrachud delivered a comprehensive dissent, holding the entire Act unconstitutional as a fraud on the Constitution for bypassing the Rajya Sabha as a Money Bill.

provisions.title: Entire Act (specifically Sections 7, 33, 47, 57)
provisions.relevance: Upheld for state welfare delivery, but stripped of private corporate exploitation under Section 57.

provisions.title: Right to Privacy and Dignity
provisions.relevance: Applied via proportionality test to invalidate private telecom and banking linkage mandates.

provisions.title: Definition of Money Bills
provisions.relevance: Majority held the welfare spending core satisfied Article 110 (referred to larger bench in Rojer Mathew).

84.overview: The Finance Act, 2017 amended multiple central enactments, merging several statutory tribunals and delegating absolute power to the Central Government to frame rules regarding qualifications, appointments, tenure, and removal of tribunal presiding officers. The amendments were challenged by bar associations as a grave encroachment on judicial independence.
84.issues: Whether the provisions of Part XIV of the Finance Act, 2017 and the Tribunal Rules, 2017 compromise judicial independence, and whether the Finance Act, 2017 could be validly passed as a Money Bill under Article 110.
84.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down the Tribunal Rules, 2017 framed under the Finance Act, 2017 as unconstitutional for compromising judicial independence. The Court held that search-cum-selection committees must have judicial dominance and referred the Money Bill question to a 7-judge Bench.
key_findings: Tribunals perform essential judicial functions and adjudicate disputes involving the government; they must possess the same institutional independence as traditional courts.
The Tribunal Rules, 2017 gave overwhelming majority and control to executive secretaries on search-cum-selection committees, violating the basic structure of judicial independence.
Search-cum-selection committees for tribunals must be headed by the Chief Justice of India or a nominee Supreme Court judge with decisive casting vote.
Short tenures of three years for tribunal members compromise adjudicatory impartiality; tenures must be fixed at a minimum of five years.
The Central Government was directed to carry out an independent 'Judicial Impact Assessment' of all statutory tribunals across India.
The Court referred the question of whether an ordinary legislation containing tribunal reforms can be certified and passed as a 'Money Bill' under Article 110 to a 7-judge Bench.
Directed the constitution of a National Tribunals Commission to operate as an independent umbrella body overseeing tribunal administration.

provisions.title: Part XIV: Tribunal reforms
provisions.relevance: Subordinated to judicial independence review; rules framed thereunder struck down.

provisions.title: Money Bills
provisions.relevance: Doubts expressed regarding whether tribunal restructuring can qualify as a Money Bill; referred to 7-judge bench.

provisions.title: Separation of powers
provisions.relevance: Enforced to mandate judicial dominance on tribunal appointment committees.

85.overview: Following the Supreme Court's ruling in MBA-IV (2020) striking down executive-dominated tribunal rules, Parliament enacted the Tribunals Reforms (Rationalisation and Conditions of Service) Ordinance, 2021, re-enacting the very same provisions (minimum age of 50 years, 4-year tenure, and selection committees) that had been declared unconstitutional by the Court.
85.issues: Whether the legislature can directly override and re-enact provisions declared unconstitutional by a judicial verdict without curing the underlying constitutional infirmities.
85.holding: By a 2:1 majority, a 3-judge Bench struck down the provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Ordinance, 2021 regarding 4-year tenure and minimum age limit of 50 years as unconstitutional and void. The Court held that the legislature cannot overrule a judicial declaration of law without removing the constitutional defect.
key_findings: The legislature has the power to enact a validating law, but it can do so only by removing the underlying defect pointed out by the court.
The legislature cannot simply re-enact the very same provision that was previously declared unconstitutional by a coordinate judicial bench; doing so violates the separation of powers.
A minimum age threshold of 50 years for appointment as tribunal members discriminates against meritorious young advocates and compromises talent acquisition.
A 4-year tenure is too short and creates insecurity of tenure, undermining adjudicatory independence and encouraging executive subservience.
Tenure of tribunal members must be at least five years to ensure institutional stability and continuity.
Judicial orders declaring fundamental rights and basic structure principles cannot be defeated by repetitive statutory enactments.
Reaffirmed that access to an independent, competent justice system is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

provisions.title: Sections 3(1), 3(7), 5, 7(1)
provisions.relevance: Provisions prescribing 4-year tenure and 50-year age bar struck down as unconstitutional.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Applied against legislative arbitrariness re-enacting judicially invalidated statutory clauses.

provisions.title: Separation of judiciary from executive
provisions.relevance: Bedrock principle preventing legislative overrides of judicial pronouncements.

86.overview: Dr. Jacob Puliyel, former member of the National Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (NTAGI), filed a PIL under Article 32 challenging coercive COVID-19 vaccine mandates issued by various state governments, which restricted unvaccinated individuals from accessing public transport, workplaces, and markets, and sought publication of clinical trial data.
86.issues: Whether state vaccine mandates violate bodily autonomy and personal integrity under Article 21, and whether the Union Government is obligated to make clinical trial data and adverse events following immunization (AEFI) publicly accessible.
86.holding: A 2-judge Bench held that bodily integrity and personal autonomy are protected under Article 21, and no individual can be forcibly vaccinated against their will. The Court held that coercive vaccine mandates issued by state governments were disproportionate and directed the Union Government to publish disaggregated AEFI clinical data.
key_findings: Bodily integrity is protected under Article 21, and an individual has the constitutional right to refuse medical treatment or vaccination.
The State has a legitimate interest in protecting public health and controlling communicable epidemics under its police power.

However, when scientific data demonstrated that vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals transmit the virus at comparable rates, denying unvaccinated persons access to public places was disproportionate under Article 14 and 21.
All coercive state vaccine mandates restricting unvaccinated citizens from accessing public facilities, transport, or employment were declared unenforceable.
The Union Government's vaccination policy was held reasonable and scientifically grounded, but voluntary uptake must remain the governing principle.
The Government of India was directed to make all disaggregated clinical trial data and reported adverse events following immunization (AEFI) publicly accessible on an open domain.
Transparency in medical data fosters public trust and reinforces democratic accountability in public health administration.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty (Bodily Integrity)
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to protect bodily autonomy and the right of informed medical choice against coercive state mandates.

provisions.title: Equality before law - Proportionality
provisions.relevance: Applied to strike down restrictions on unvaccinated individuals as scientifically ungrounded and disproportionate.

87.overview: Multiple LGBTQ+ couples filed writ petitions under Article 32 seeking the legal recognition of same-sex marriage under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, and challenging the gender-binary provisions of the Act. Petitioners argued that denying queer persons the right to marry violated their rights to equality, non-discrimination, privacy, and personal autonomy.
87.issues: Whether there is a fundamental right to marry under the Constitution of India, and whether the Special Marriage Act, 1954 can be judicially interpreted or gender-neutralized to include same-sex and queer marriages.
87.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench held (unanimously) that there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry under the Constitution, and that reading same-sex marriage into the Special Marriage Act is a legislative function outside the judicial sphere. However, the Court unanimously recognized the fundamental right of queer couples to enter into union, directing the Union to constitute a high-powered committee.
key_findings: There is no unqualified fundamental right to marry recognized under Part III of the Constitution; marriage is a creature of statute and personal law.

Interpreting the Special Marriage Act to include same-sex unions would require extensive redrafting of intertwined statutory codes (succession, adoption, maintenance, domestic violence), which lies solely within the legislative domain of Parliament.
Queer and transgender individuals possess the fundamental right under Article 21 to enter into consensual cohabiting partnerships and unions free from state discrimination.
The State is under a positive obligation to ensure that queer couples are protected from harassment, violence, and discrimination by families and law enforcement agencies.
By a 3:2 majority, the Court held that queer couples do not have a constitutional right to joint adoption under Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) regulations.
The Union Government's assurance to constitute a high-powered committee headed by the Cabinet Secretary to grant socio-economic rights, banking, and insurance benefits to queer couples was recorded.
CJI Chandrachud and Justice S.K. Kaul delivered powerful opinions affirming that queer partnerships are entitled to full constitutional recognition and civil protection.

provisions.title: Civil marriage enactment
provisions.relevance: Held to be incapable of judicial redrafting for same-sex marriages without parliamentary legislation.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as protecting consensual relational autonomy, cohabitation, and freedom from state harassment for LGBTQ+ persons.

provisions.title: Equality and non-discrimination
provisions.relevance: Applied to prohibit discriminatory administrative harassment of queer partnerships.

88.overview: Cox and Kings Ltd. entered into agreements with SAP India for software licensing and maintenance. When commercial disputes arose, Cox and Kings invoked arbitration and sought to join SAP SE (the German parent company) as a party to the arbitral proceedings, despite the parent company not being a formal signatory to the arbitration agreement. A 5-judge Constitution Bench was constituted to settle the validity of the 'Group of Companies' doctrine.
88.issues: Whether the 'Group of Companies' doctrine has legal standing in Indian arbitration law under Section 7 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and on what basis a non-signatory corporate affiliate can be bound by an arbitration agreement.
88.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench unanimously upheld the validity and applicability of the 'Group of Companies' doctrine in Indian arbitration law. The Court held that a non-signatory corporate entity can be bound by an arbitration agreement based on mutual intent, commercial involvement, and commonality of subject-matter.
key_findings: The Group of Companies doctrine is an integral part of modern international arbitration jurisprudence and is recognized under Section 7 of the Arbitration Act.
The doctrine is grounded in the mutual commercial intention of the parties, not on lifting the corporate veil or fraud.
A non-signatory corporate affiliate may be joined as a party to arbitration if its active conduct demonstrates an intention to be bound by the underlying contract.

Factors to determine inclusion: (1) direct relationship with a signatory; (2) commonality of subject-matter; (3) composite nature of the commercial transaction; and (4) active participation in contract negotiation or performance.
Mere corporate affiliation or holding-subsidiary relationship is insufficient on its own to bind a non-signatory affiliate.
The referral court under Section 8 or 11 must leave the complex factual inquiry of whether a non-signatory is bound to the arbitral tribunal under Section 16.
Overruled earlier rigid formulations that required piercing of the corporate veil to join non-signatories in arbitration.

provisions.title: Arbitration agreement
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to encompass non-signatory group entities through mutual commercial intention.

provisions.title: Referral and appointment of arbitrators
provisions.relevance: Restricted referral court review to prima facie examination, leaving group joinder to the arbitral tribunal.

provisions.title: Competence of arbitral tribunal to rule on jurisdiction
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as the primary forum to decide whether non-signatory affiliates are proper parties.

89.overview: Following conflicting decisions regarding unstamped or insufficiently stamped arbitration agreements, a 5-judge Constitution Bench in N.N. Global-I held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is void and unenforceable. A larger 7-judge Constitution Bench was constituted on a curative reference to authoritatively determine whether an unstamped contract renders the arbitration clause non-existent at the referral stage.
89.issues: Whether an unstamped or insufficiently stamped arbitration agreement is void ab initio under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, and whether referral courts under Section 8 or 11 of the Arbitration Act can examine stamping before appointing an arbitrator.
89.holding: A unanimous 7-judge Constitution Bench overruled the 5-judge bench decision in N.N. Global-I. The Court held that an unstamped or insufficiently stamped agreement is not void ab initio, but merely inadmissible in evidence, and that the defect is curable. The arbitral tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to decide stamping issues under Section 16.
key_findings: Non-stamping of an underlying commercial contract is a curable fiscal defect under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899; it does not render the agreement void ab initio.
The principle of separability under Section 16 of the Arbitration Act establishes that the arbitration clause is a distinct agreement independent of the underlying contract.
At the referral stage under Section 8 or 11, the court's scrutiny is strictly limited to examining the prima facie 'existence' of the arbitration agreement.
Objections regarding non-stamping, insufficiency of stamp duty, and impounding must be decided by the arbitral tribunal under Section 16.
Allowing referral courts to conduct detailed stamp duty inquiries would defeat the core statutory objective of minimal judicial interference under Section 5.
Overruled SMS Tea Estates (2011), Garware Wall Ropes (2019), and N.N. Global-I (2023) to establish India as a pro-arbitration jurisdiction.
Harmonized the revenue collection mandate of the Stamp Act with the speedy dispute resolution mandate of the Arbitration Act.

provisions.title: Appointment of arbitrators - Examination of existence of agreement
provisions.relevance: Interpreted strictly to confine court review to formal existence, leaving stamp duty issues to the arbitrator.

provisions.title: Instruments not duly stamped inadmissible in evidence
provisions.relevance: Held to be a curable evidentiary bar rather than a nullification of legal existence.

provisions.title: Minimal judicial interference and competence-competence
provisions.relevance: Applied as core pillars ensuring referral courts do not delay arbitration for fiscal defects.

90.overview: Mining companies, led by the Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL) and Tata Steel, challenged tax levies on mineral-bearing lands imposed by the State of Bihar under the Bihar Land Reforms Act. The companies argued that royalty paid on minerals constitutes a tax, and that Parliament's enactment of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) denuded State Legislatures of the power to tax mineral rights.
90.issues: Whether royalty on minerals is in the nature of a tax, and whether Parliament's legislative power under Entry 54 of List I and the MMDR Act denudes State Legislatures of their constitutional power to tax mineral-bearing lands under Entry 49 and Entry 50 of List II.
90.holding: A 9-judge Constitution Bench (8:1 majority) delivered a historic ruling holding that 'royalty is not a tax'. The Court ruled that State Legislatures possess the constitutional power to tax mineral rights and mineral-bearing lands under Entry 49 and Entry 50 of List II, and that the MMDR Act does not eclipse the states' taxation powers.
key_findings: Royalty is a consideration paid by a mining lessee to the mineral owner for parting with the mineral resource; it is not a compulsory exaction of tax.
The 7-judge bench decision in India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990), to the extent it observed that royalty is a tax, was an apparent typographical error and was formally overruled.
Entry 50 of List II confers exclusive legislative power on State Legislatures to levy taxes on mineral rights, subject only to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law.
Entry 49 of List II authorizes states to tax lands, including mineral-bearing lands, based on the economic value or yield of the land.
Parliament's regulatory power over mines and minerals under Entry 54 of List I and the MMDR Act, 1957 does not include the power to tax; regulatory power cannot swallow taxation power.
States have constitutional fiscal autonomy under the federal framework to mobilize revenues from natural resources within their territorial boundaries.
Justice B.V. Nagarathna delivered a lone dissent, warning that uncoordinated state levies on minerals could create economic chaos and inter-state trade fragmentation.

provisions.title: Taxes on mineral rights
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as conferring sovereign taxation competence on State Legislatures.

provisions.title: Taxes on lands and buildings
provisions.relevance: Held to authorize state taxation of mineral-bearing lands based on mineral yield.

provisions.title: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act
provisions.relevance: Held not to strip states of their constitutional taxing powers under the State List.

91.overview: Former Maharashtra Chief Minister A.R. Antulay was prosecuted for corruption under the Prevention of Corruption Act. In an earlier appeal in 1984, the Supreme Court suo motu transferred his trial from the Special Judge to the Bombay High Court to ensure an expedited trial. Antulay challenged the transfer order, contending that it deprived him of his statutory right of appeal to the High Court under Section 9 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952 and Section 406 CrPC.
91.issues: Whether the Supreme Court has the jurisdiction to transfer a criminal trial to a court without statutory jurisdiction, and whether an order of the Supreme Court that violates an accused's fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 21 can be recalled by the Court under its inherent powers.
91.holding: A 7-judge Constitution Bench held that the Supreme Court's earlier transfer order was void ab initio and without jurisdiction. The Court held that even the Supreme Court cannot deprive a citizen of a statutory right of appeal, and that an order violating fundamental rights can be recalled ex debito justitiae (giving birth to Curative Petitions).
key_findings: No judicial order, even an order passed by the Supreme Court of India, can violate the fundamental rights of a citizen under Article 14 or 21.
A court cannot confer jurisdiction upon a forum where no statutory jurisdiction exists; jurisdiction can only be created by competent legislative enactment.
By transferring the trial directly to the High Court, the Supreme Court deprived the accused of his valuable statutory right of first appeal to the High Court.
Deprivation of a statutory right of appeal constitutes an arbitrary classification violating equality under Article 14.
The maxim 'actus curiae neminem gravabit' (an act of the court shall prejudice no one) mandates that courts must rectify their own errors.
The Supreme Court possesses inherent jurisdiction ex debito justitiae to recall and set aside its own judgment if passed per incuriam or in violation of fundamental rights.
This decision created the theoretical foundation for the doctrine of Curative Petitions later institutionalized in Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002).

provisions.title: Equality and fair procedure
provisions.relevance: Enforced to hold that judicial orders cannot strip an accused of statutory appellate forums.

provisions.title: Power of Supreme Court to transfer cases
provisions.relevance: Held not to authorize transfer to a court lacking original statutory competence.

provisions.title: Complete justice power
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as incapable of being used to bypass substantive statutory rights of citizens.

92.overview: Mithu and other life convicts challenged the constitutional validity of Section 303 of the Indian Penal Code. Section 303 mandated a compulsory death penalty for any person who commits murder while undergoing a sentence of life imprisonment, leaving the sentencing judge with zero discretion to award life imprisonment.
92.issues: Whether Section 303 of the Indian Penal Code, providing a mandatory death penalty for murders committed by life convicts, violates Article 14 and Article 21 of the Constitution.
92.holding: A unanimous 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down Section 303 of the Indian Penal Code as unconstitutional and void. The Court held that a mandatory death penalty deprives the sentencing judge of judicial discretion and violates Articles 14 and 21.
key_findings: A mandatory death penalty deprives the judiciary of its essential sentencing function to weigh individual aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
Section 303 creates an irrational and arbitrary classification between life convicts and ordinary convicts committing murder, violating Article 14.
A life convict who has been on parole for years or whose original conviction was under appeal cannot be subjected to automatic execution without sentencing hearing.
Procedure established by law under Article 21 must be just, fair, and reasonable; a law that prescribes automatic death without a hearing on sentence under Section 235(2) CrPC is barbarous and void.
The legislature cannot mandate automatic hanging without allowing the convict to demonstrate mitigating factors, remorse, or rehabilitation.
All pending and future trials for murder committed by life convicts must be tried and sentenced under Section 302 IPC (discretionary death or life imprisonment).
Chief Justice Chandrachud observed that Section 303 was an archaic colonial relic drafted to protect British prison wardens, lacking any rational contemporary justification.

provisions.title: Punishment for murder by life-convict
provisions.relevance: Struck down in its entirety as unconstitutional and void under Articles 14 and 21.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Applied to mandate fair sentencing hearings and individual consideration before awarding death.

provisions.title: Hearing on question of sentence
provisions.relevance: Affirmed as a mandatory statutory requirement that cannot be bypassed by mandatory capital statutes.

93.overview: Gian Kaur and her husband were convicted under Section 306 IPC for abetting the suicide of their daughter-in-law, Kulwant Kaur. The appellants challenged their conviction, relying on the Supreme Court's 2-judge bench decision in P. Rathinam (1994), which had held that Section 309 IPC (attempt to commit suicide) was unconstitutional because the right to life under Article 21 includes the 'right to die'.
93.issues: Whether the right to life under Article 21 includes the 'right to die', and whether Section 306 IPC (abetment of suicide) and Section 309 IPC (attempt to commit suicide) are unconstitutional.
93.holding: A 5-judge Constitution Bench overruled P. Rathinam and upheld the constitutional validity of Section 306 and Section 309 of the Indian Penal Code. The Court held that the right to life under Article 21 does not include the right to terminate life or commit suicide.
key_findings: Article 21 guarantees the protection of life and personal liberty; 'life' signifies human existence with dignity and cannot be construed to include its own extinction.
The right to life is a natural, positive right; an unnatural termination of life (suicide) is antithetical to the concept of the right to life.
Section 306 IPC (punishing abetment of suicide) is constitutionally valid and does not violate Articles 14 or 21.
Section 309 IPC (criminalizing attempt to commit suicide) was held constitutionally valid (though Parliament subsequently decriminalized it via the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017).

The Court drew a fundamental legal distinction between 'euthanasia / premature termination of life' and 'the right of a dying patient in a vegetative state to die with dignity' by withdrawing artificial life support.
Passive euthanasia in vegetative irreversible states is not the termination of life, but permitting the natural process of death to occur with dignity.
P. Rathinam was overruled to the extent it held that Article 21 incorporates a fundamental right to die.

provisions.title: Abetment of suicide
provisions.relevance: Constitutional validity upheld as a vital penal deterrent protecting vulnerable lives.

provisions.title: Attempt to commit suicide
provisions.relevance: Upheld as constitutionally valid, overruling the contrary finding in P. Rathinam.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to hold that the right to life does not include an unnatural right to extinguish life.

94.overview: Lawyers and bar associations challenged circulars issued by the Union Law Minister seeking advance consent of additional High Court judges for transfer to other states, as well as the non-extension of additional judges. The petitions, known as the First Judges Case, raised monumental questions regarding judicial independence, executive appointments, and legal standing.
94.issues: What is the meaning of 'consultation' in Articles 124(2) and 217(1) of the Constitution, whether the executive or the Chief Justice of India holds primacy in judicial appointments, and who has standing to maintain a PIL.
94.holding: A 7-judge Constitution Bench held that 'consultation' does not mean 'concurrence', and that the Central Government holds primacy in judicial appointments (later overruled in the Second Judges Case). However, the Court made historic breakthroughs in procedural jurisprudence by dramatically liberalizing locus standi and founding Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India.
key_findings: The majority held that under Articles 124 and 217, the executive holds ultimate primacy in judicial appointments, and consultation with the CJI is not binding.
This restrictive holding on appointments was subsequently overruled in the Second Judges Case (1993) and Third Judges Case (1998).
On procedure, the Court made a revolutionary breakthrough by democratizing the doctrine of locus standi in Indian constitutional law.

Where a legal injury is caused to a person or class of persons who by reason of poverty, disability, or socially disadvantaged position cannot approach the court, any public-spirited member of the public can maintain an action under Article 32 or 226.
The rule of strict traditional standing was discarded in favour of representative public interest litigation (PIL).
State secrecy and claims of Crown Privilege under Section 123 of the Evidence Act regarding cabinet documents on judicial appointments were rejected.
Justice P.N. Bhagwati articulated the transformative role of the judiciary as an instrument of social justice for the downtrodden.

provisions.title: Writ jurisdiction - Liberalization of Locus Standi
provisions.relevance: Revolutionized standing rules, establishing the foundational architecture of Public Interest Litigation in India.

provisions.title: Judicial appointments
provisions.relevance: Executive primacy affirmed by majority (later overruled in Second Judges Case).

provisions.title: Evidence as to affairs of State
provisions.relevance: State privilege claims over judicial transfer correspondence rejected, promoting administrative transparency.

225.overview: Socialist leader Raj Narain filed an election petition before the Allahabad High Court challenging the election of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi from the Rae Bareli parliamentary constituency in the 1971 Lok Sabha elections. The petition alleged extensive corrupt electoral practices under Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
225.issues: Whether Prime Minister Indira Gandhi committed corrupt electoral practices under Section 123(7) of the Representation of the People Act by utilizing gazetted government servants (Yashpal Kapoor) and state machinery (rostrums and police) for election campaign work.
225.holding: Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha of the Allahabad High Court delivered a historic verdict holding Indira Gandhi guilty of corrupt electoral practices under Section 123(7) of the RP Act. The High Court set aside her election to the Lok Sabha and disqualified her from contesting elective office for six years.
key_findings: The Prime Minister is an elected representative under the Constitution and is subject to the same election laws as any ordinary citizen of India.

The appointment of Yashpal Kapoor, an officer on special duty in the Prime Minister's Secretariat, as election agent before his formal resignation was gazetted constituted obtaining assistance from a government servant under Section 123(7).

The construction of election rostrums, supply of electricity, and deployment of state police and administrative machinery by the UP Government for election meetings constituted corrupt electoral practice under Section 123(7).
The election of Indira Gandhi to the Lok Sabha from the Rae Bareli constituency was declared null and void.
Under Section 8A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, she was disqualified from holding elective public office for a statutory period of six years.
The High Court granted a temporary stay of 20 days to enable the respondent to appeal to the Supreme Court.
This historic verdict precipitated the declaration of the National Emergency on 25 June 1975, altering modern Indian political and constitutional history.

provisions.title: Corrupt practices - Obtaining assistance of government servants
provisions.relevance: Directly applied to invalidate the parliamentary election of the Prime Minister.

provisions.title: Disqualification on ground of corrupt practices
provisions.relevance: Enforced to impose a six-year disqualification from contesting elections.

226.overview: The applicant, Zameer Ahmad, challenged the invocation of the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986 based on a single isolated criminal case, seeking bail and challenging arbitrary police invocation of gangster laws.
226.issues: Whether criminal prosecution under the UP Gangsters Act can be sustained on the basis of a single criminal case, and what principles govern bail under the stringent provisions of Section 19(4) of the Act.
226.holding: The Allahabad High Court held that while Gangsters Act proceedings can be initiated based on a single case if the statutory gang chart discloses organized anti-social activity, bail must be granted when the twin conditions under Section 19(4) are satisfied and the applicant is already on bail in the substantive predicate case.
key_findings: The UP Gangsters Act is a special enactment to curb organized crime syndicates; its provisions must be applied with care and not as a tool of routine police harassment.
Proceedings under the Gangsters Act can legally be instituted on the basis of a single FIR, provided the gang chart demonstrates organized gang activity.
Under Section 19(4) of the Gangsters Act, bail is subject to twin conditions: reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and not likely to commit offences while on bail.
When the accused has already been enlarged on bail in the substantive predicate case forming the basis of the gang chart, the rigorous bar on bail stands significantly diluted.
Mechanical invocation of the Gangsters Act without demonstrating membership of a defined criminal gang violates Article 21.
Police authorities must strictly adhere to the Gangsters Rules, 2021 regarding approval of gang charts by the District Magistrate.
The applicant was granted bail subject to personal bonds and cooperation with trial.

provisions.act: UP Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986
provisions.title: Definition of gang and penalty for gangster
provisions.relevance: Subjected to strict scrutiny regarding gang chart approval and predicate offence nexus.

provisions.act: UP Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986
provisions.title: Modified bail provisions (Twin conditions)
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to facilitate bail where the applicant is already on bail in the substantive case.

227.overview: Dr. Kafeel Khan, a pediatrician at BRD Medical College, Gorakhpur, was detained under the National Security Act (NSA), 1980 by an order of the District Magistrate, Aligarh, for delivering a speech during anti-CAA/NRC protests at Aligarh Muslim University (AMU). His mother filed a habeas corpus petition under Article 226 before the Allahabad High Court.
227.issues: Whether the speech delivered by Dr. Kafeel Khan posed a threat to public order under the National Security Act, and whether his preventive detention was arbitrary, illegal, and violative of Articles 21 and 22.
227.holding: A Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Chief Justice Govind Mathur and Justice Saumitra Dayal Singh) quashed the NSA detention order and directed his immediate release. The Court held that a reading of the full speech showed that it promoted national unity and peaceful dissent, and did not incite violence or disrupt public order.
key_findings: Preventive detention under the National Security Act is an extraordinary executive power that curtails liberty without trial; it must be exercised with extreme circumspection.
The subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority must be founded on objective, relevant material showing a real threat to 'public order'.
The District Magistrate relied on selective excerpts taken out of context; a complete reading of the speech showed it did not promote hatred or communal disharmony.
The speech emphasized national unity, non-violence, and constitutional values, and did not incite any violence in Aligarh.
The detention order was passed two months after the speech without any proximate nexus or contemporaneous disturbance of public peace.
Failure to supply legible copies of detention material and rejection of his representation without reasoned consideration violated Article 22(5).
The detention was held to be illegal, arbitrary, and an abuse of preventive detention power.

provisions.title: Power to make orders detaining certain persons
provisions.relevance: Detention order quashed as perverse and lacking factual basis for public order disturbance.

provisions.title: Right to make representation against preventive detention
provisions.relevance: Enforced to hold detention void due to delayed and uncommunicated representation disposal.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Vindicated by ordering the immediate release of the wrongfully detained physician.

228.overview: Naz Foundation, an NGO working with HIV/AIDS prevention, filed a writ petition under Article 226 before the Delhi High Court challenging the constitutional validity of Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code to the extent it criminalized consensual sexual acts between adults in private.
228.issues: Whether Section 377 IPC violates Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 of the Constitution by criminalizing consensual sexual acts between adults in private.
228.holding: A Division Bench of the Delhi High Court (Chief Justice A.P. Shah and Justice S. Muralidhar) delivered a historic verdict reading down Section 377 IPC to decriminalize consensual sexual acts between adults in private, establishing foundational constitutional principles of inclusivity and dignity.
key_findings: Constitutional morality, not popular or majoritarian morality, must guide the interpretation of fundamental rights.
Section 377 criminalizes an unchangeable attribute of personhood and identity, driving sexual minorities underground and impairing HIV/AIDS healthcare.
Consensual sexual conduct between adults in private is protected under the fundamental right to privacy and human dignity under Article 21.
Section 377 discriminates on the ground of 'sex' under Article 15(1), which includes discrimination based on sexual orientation.
The provision is arbitrary and irrational under Article 14, lacking any legitimate state interest in policing private adult consensual intimacy.
Dignity and equality are foundational values of the Indian Constitution that protect every citizen, especially vulnerable minorities.
Although temporarily reversed by the Supreme Court in Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013), this judgment was fully vindicated and reaffirmed by the 5-judge Constitution Bench in Navtej Singh Johar (2018).

provisions.title: Unnatural offences
provisions.relevance: Historic first judicial verdict reading down the penal provision to decriminalize consensual adult acts.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to establish human dignity and private consensual autonomy for LGBTQ+ citizens.

provisions.title: Equality and non-discrimination
provisions.relevance: Applied to prohibit discriminatory criminalization based on innate sexual orientation.

229.overview: Swedish telecommunications giant Ericsson held Standard Essential Patents (SEPs) for 2G and 3G cellular technologies and sued Indian phone manufacturers (Micromax, Intex) for patent infringement. In response, the manufacturers complained to the Competition Commission of India (CCI), alleging that Ericsson abused its dominant position by demanding unreasonable and discriminatory royalties (violating FRAND terms). Ericsson challenged the CCI's jurisdiction before the Delhi High Court.
229.issues: Whether the Competition Commission of India (CCI) has jurisdiction under the Competition Act, 2002 to investigate patent licensing practices and allegations of anti-competitive conduct in relation to Standard Essential Patents (SEPs) governed by the Patents Act, 1970.
229.holding: A Division Bench of the Delhi High Court held that the Patents Act, 1970 is a specialized enactment governing patent rights, and its comprehensive provisions on compulsory licensing and abuse under Chapter XVI prevail over the general anti-trust jurisdiction of the Competition Act, 2002. The CCI's proceedings against Ericsson were held to be without jurisdiction.
key_findings: The Patents Act, 1970 and the Competition Act, 2002 are both special statutes, but in relation to patents and patentee licensing conduct, the Patents Act is the specialized code.
Chapter XVI of the Patents Act (Sections 82 to 94) comprehensively regulates compulsory licensing, revocation of patents, and abusive conditions imposed by patentees.
Applying the principle of lex specialis derogat legi generali, the specialized mechanism under the Patents Act excludes the jurisdiction of the Competition Commission of India.
The Controller of Patents is the specialized statutory authority equipped to evaluate licensing terms, reasonable royalties, and working of patents.
The CCI cannot initiate parallel anti-trust investigations into matters squarely regulated by the Controller of Patents under Chapter XVI.
Section 3(5) of the Competition Act expressly preserves the right of any person to restrain patent infringement or impose reasonable conditions necessary for protecting patent rights.
The proceedings initiated by the CCI against Ericsson were quashed for lack of statutory jurisdiction.

provisions.title: Chapter XVI: Working of Patents and Compulsory Licences
provisions.relevance: Held to be a self-contained specialized code overriding general competition commission inquiries.

provisions.title: Sections 3, 4, 19
provisions.relevance: Jurisdiction excluded over Standard Essential Patent licensing practices covered by the Patents Act.

230.overview: Luxury French footwear designer Christian Louboutin filed a commercial suit before the Delhi High Court seeking permanent injunction against shoe traders in Delhi for infringing his registered trademark for the iconic 'Red Sole' mark (a distinctive red lacquered sole on high-heeled women's shoes).
230.issues: Whether a single colour applied to the sole of a shoe can qualify as a valid 'trademark' under Section 2(1)(m) and Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, and whether Louboutin could claim trademark infringement based on a single colour.
230.holding: The Delhi High Court held that under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the statutory definition of a 'mark' includes a 'combination of colours', but not a single colour on its own. Consequently, trademark infringement under Section 29 could not be sustained on a single colour, though passing off remedies remained available.
key_findings: Section 2(1)(m) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 defines a 'mark' to include a 'combination of colours'; it deliberately does not mention a single isolated colour.
A single colour applied to a functional part of a product (shoe sole) cannot prima facie constitute a valid trademark under the statutory scheme.
Monopolizing a single colour would lead to anti-competitive depletion of the colour palette for competing manufacturers.
The registration of a single colour mark under Section 29 does not confer an absolute right to prevent others from using that colour unless a unique combination of colours is established.
However, if a single colour has acquired extraordinary secondary meaning and distinctive reputation among consumers, a common law action for 'passing off' is maintainable.
The Court held that the suit could not be decreed for statutory infringement, distinguishing Indian trademark law from US and European single-colour trademark jurisprudence.
Set a landmark precedent on the limits of non-conventional single-colour trademarks under Indian intellectual property law.

provisions.title: Section 2(1)(m) & 2(1)(zb)
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to hold that 'mark' encompasses a combination of colours but excludes a single colour.

provisions.title: Infringement of registered trademarks
provisions.relevance: Held inapplicable to enforce monopoly over a single colour sole.

231.overview: Film financier Bharat Shanti Lal Shah was prosecuted under the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 (MCOCA) for alleged links with underworld organized crime syndicates (Chhota Shakeel gang). The constitutional validity of several provisions of MCOCA, including wiretapping powers and admissibility of intercepted communications, was challenged before the Bombay High Court.
231.issues: Whether MCOCA is within the legislative competence of the State Legislature, and whether the interception of communications under Sections 13 to 16 violates the fundamental right to privacy under Article 21.
231.holding: A Division Bench of the Bombay High Court upheld the legislative competence of the State Legislature to enact MCOCA under Entries 1 and 2 of List II (Public Order and Police). The Court upheld wiretapping provisions subject to strict procedural safeguards, but struck down Section 2(1)(d) to the extent it included promoting insurgency.
key_findings: The State Legislature possesses legislative competence under List II, Entry 1 (Public Order) and Entry 2 (Police) to enact special legislation targeting organized crime syndicates.
Interception of wire, electronic, or oral communications under Section 13 to 16 of MCOCA is an extraordinary investigative tool justified by the sophisticated nature of mafia syndicates.
Interception of communications implicates the fundamental right to privacy under Article 21 and must strictly satisfy statutory safeguards.
Authorizations for wiretapping must be granted by an officer not below the rank of Additional Chief Secretary (Home) with recorded reasons of necessity.
Evidence obtained through illegal, unauthorized, or procedural non-compliant wiretapping is inadmissible in evidence under MCOCA.
Section 2(1)(d) was read down so that ordinary political protests and non-organized criminal activities cannot be brought within the draconic net of MCOCA.
The Supreme Court subsequently affirmed the Bombay High Court's ruling, cementing MCOCA as a model for state anti-organized crime statutes.

provisions.title: Sections 13 to 16: Interception of wire and electronic communications
provisions.relevance: Upheld as constitutionally valid subject to rigorous executive authorization safeguards.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Applied to balance telephonic privacy against state security requirements in organized crime probes.

232.overview: Anupam Rasayan India Ltd. imported specialized chemical intermediaries used in manufacturing agrochemicals and pharmaceuticals. Customs authorities classified the imports under a higher tariff heading carrying higher customs duty, contrary to an Advance Ruling previously issued by the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings (CAAR). The company approached the Bombay High Court.
232.issues: Whether an Advance Ruling issued by the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings (CAAR) under Section 28J of the Customs Act, 1962 is binding on jurisdictional customs field formations across India.
232.holding: The Bombay High Court held that an Advance Ruling issued under Section 28J of the Customs Act is statutorily binding on the Commissioner of Customs and all subordinate customs officers across all ports in India with respect to that applicant and the goods in question, unless the law or facts have changed.
key_findings: The purpose of advance rulings in customs law is to provide certainty, predictability, and reduce protracted litigation in international trade.
Under Section 28J of the Customs Act, 1962, an advance ruling is binding on the applicant and all customs officers across India concerning the goods evaluated.
Jurisdictional field formations cannot disregard or sit in appeal over an advance ruling issued by CAAR by unilaterally raising reassessment notices.
If the customs department is aggrieved by an advance ruling, the only legal remedy available is to prefer a statutory appeal under Section 28KA to the High Court.
Unilateral reassessment by customs authorities contrary to a binding advance ruling is arbitrary, illegal, and destructive of commercial ease of doing business.
Customs authorities were directed to release the imported chemical consignments in accordance with the classification determined in the advance ruling.
Reaffirmed the principle of institutional administrative discipline in revenue administration.

provisions.title: Applicability of advance ruling
provisions.relevance: Interpreted to hold advance rulings strictly binding on all field formations across India.

provisions.title: Writ jurisdiction of High Court
provisions.relevance: Exercised to enforce statutory compliance and quash contrary departmental show-cause notices.

233.overview: Following the declaration of results of the West Bengal Legislative Assembly elections in May 2021, widespread post-poll violence broke out across the state, resulting in killings, gang-rapes, destruction of homes, and mass displacement of opposition political workers. Multiple PILs were filed before the Calcutta High Court seeking an independent probe into state police inaction.
233.issues: Whether systemic post-poll violence and state police inaction violate fundamental rights under Article 21, and whether an independent court-monitored investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is warranted.
233.holding: A 5-judge Special Bench of the Calcutta High Court ordered a court-monitored investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) into all heinous cases of murder, rape, and unnatural deaths, and constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT) monitored by retired judges for other serious offences.
key_findings: The State Government owes a non-negotiable constitutional duty under Article 21 to protect the life, liberty, and property of all citizens irrespective of political allegiance.
Systemic violence, forced displacement, and destruction of livelihoods following democratic elections represent a complete breakdown of constitutional trust.
The findings of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) committee revealed widespread police apathy, refusal to register FIRs, and state complicity.
When the local police apparatus is perceived as partisan or compromised, an independent agency must be brought in to restore public confidence in the administration of justice.
All cases involving murder, rape, and attempted rape were transferred to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) for court-monitored investigation.
A 3-member Special Investigation Team (SIT) was constituted to investigate other cases of arson, loot, and physical violence, monitored by a retired Supreme Court/High Court judge.
The State of West Bengal was directed to provide immediate monetary compensation, medical rehabilitation, and security to displaced victims.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
provisions.relevance: Enforced to mandate an independent CBI probe where local police failed to protect citizens from political violence.

provisions.title: Writ powers of High Court
provisions.relevance: Exercised by a 5-judge bench to supervise an ongoing court-monitored investigation.

234.overview: A divorced woman filed an application under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (DV Act) seeking residence orders, protection, and monetary maintenance against her former husband and in-laws for domestic abuse inflicted during their marriage.
234.issues: Whether a divorced woman can institute proceedings under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 against her former husband for domestic violence committed during the subsistence of the marriage.
234.holding: The Madras High Court held that a divorced woman is fully entitled to maintain an application under the Domestic Violence Act against her former husband, provided she was in a domestic relationship with him at the time the acts of domestic violence occurred.
key_findings: The Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is a progressive, beneficial social welfare legislation enacted to provide civil protection to victimized women.
The definition of 'aggrieved person' under Section 2(a) includes any woman who 'is, or has been, in a domestic relationship' with the respondent.
The use of the words 'has been' explicitly encompasses women who were in a marital domestic relationship in the past, including divorced wives.
Subsequent divorce does not wipe out or erase the domestic violence, economic deprivation, or physical cruelty suffered during the marriage.
A divorced wife can claim maintenance, compensation, and return of streedhan under Sections 18, 19, 20, and 22 of the Act.
However, a divorced wife cannot claim a shared household right under Section 17 in a residence after the marital tie has been formally severed.
Technical procedural objections cannot be permitted to defeat the remedial objective of protecting women from economic destitution.

provisions.title: Section 2(a) & 2(f): Aggrieved person and domestic relationship
provisions.relevance: Interpreted broadly to include divorced women subjected to past violence in marriage.

provisions.act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
provisions.title: Application to Magistrate
provisions.relevance: Maintained as a valid statutory remedy available to divorced women for maintenance and compensation.

235.overview: Muslim female students in government pre-university colleges in Udupi, Karnataka, were barred from entering classrooms wearing the hijab (headscarf) pursuant to a state government order mandating adherence to prescribed college uniforms. The students challenged the order under Article 226, contending that wearing the hijab is an Essential Religious Practice (ERP) under Article 25 and an expression of privacy under Article 21.
235.issues: Whether the wearing of hijab by Muslim women is an Essential Religious Practice (ERP) under Islam protected under Article 25, and whether the prescription of school uniforms in state educational institutions violates Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 21.
235.holding: A 3-judge Bench of the Karnataka High Court dismissed the writ petitions, holding that the wearing of hijab is not an Essential Religious Practice (ERP) of Islam under Article 25. The Court upheld the power of educational institutions to prescribe a uniform dress code as a reasonable restriction promoting equality and secular harmony.
key_findings: To qualify as an Essential Religious Practice (ERP) under Article 25, the practice must be foundational to the religion such that its absence would alter the character of the faith.
The Holy Quran mentions hijab as a recommendation or culture of modesty, but wearing it is not an obligatory, essential religious tenet of Islam.
The prescription of school uniforms is a reasonable restriction on fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(a) designed to promote visual equality and fraternity among students.
Educational institutions have the institutional autonomy to prescribe uniforms in classrooms to foster an inclusive, secular learning environment.
The state government order directing College Development Committees to prescribe uniforms was gender-neutral and did not violate Article 14 or 15.
The right to education under Article 21A cannot be conditioned on an absolute right to wear non-uniform religious attire inside classrooms.
The judgment was subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court, which delivered a split 1:1 verdict in October 2022 (referred to a larger bench).

provisions.title: Freedom of conscience and religion
provisions.relevance: Evaluated under the Essential Religious Practices test; wearing of hijab held non-essential.

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression
provisions.relevance: Held subject to reasonable school uniform regulations in educational institutions.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Uniform policy upheld as promoting visual equality and secular unity in schools.

236.overview: Faheema Shirin, an undergraduate student at an affiliated college of the University of Calicut, was expelled from her women's college hostel for refusing to abide by a hostel rule that banned the use of mobile phones by female students between 6:00 PM and 10:00 PM. She approached the Kerala High Court under Article 226 challenging the restriction as discriminatory and patriarchal.
236.issues: Whether the restriction on mobile phone and internet usage in a college hostel violates the fundamental right to access information, privacy, and personal liberty under Article 21 and Article 19(1)(a).
236.holding: The Kerala High Court struck down the discriminatory hostel rule and quashed the student's expulsion. The Court held that the right to access the internet is an integral component of the Right to Education under Article 21A and the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21.
key_findings: The internet is an indispensable modern infrastructure for learning, research, education, and acquiring knowledge in the digital era.
The right to access the internet is a fundamental right forming an intrinsic part of the Right to Education (Article 21A) and Right to Life (Article 21).
College students are responsible adults; imposition of total bans on digital connectivity under the guise of discipline constitutes outdated paternalism.
The rule applied exclusively to female students in the women's hostel while male students faced no such restriction, violating gender equality under Article 14 and 15.
Hostel rules cannot infringe upon an adult citizen's fundamental right to communicate and acquire knowledge during leisure hours.
Educational authorities can frame reasonable discipline for classrooms, but cannot curtail digital access in hostel residences.
This decision pioneered the judicial recognition of internet access as a constitutional human right in India.

provisions.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
