provisions.relevance: Expanded to recognize access to the internet and digital communication as a fundamental human right.

provisions.title: Equality and non-discrimination on grounds of sex
provisions.relevance: Applied against patriarchal hostel rules imposing restrictions exclusively on female students.

provisions.title: Right to education
provisions.relevance: Harmonized with digital access as essential to modern higher education.

237.overview: The State of Gujarat appealed against the acquittal of a public servant accused under Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 in a bribery trap case. The trial court had acquitted the accused because the prosecution failed to prove an independent demand for the illegal gratification prior to the trap.
237.issues: Whether mere recovery of tainted currency notes from a public servant is sufficient to sustain a conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, or whether proof of demand of bribe is an indispensable prerequisite.
237.holding: The Gujarat High Court dismissed the state's appeal and upheld the acquittal. The Court held that proof of demand of illegal gratification is the gravamen of an offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act; mere recovery of tainted money without proof of demand cannot sustain a conviction.
key_findings: In bribery trials under the Prevention of Corruption Act, proof of demand is an indispensable condition precedent to establish guilt under Sections 7 and 13.
Mere recovery of tainted currency notes from the pocket or table of a public servant, without proof of demand, cannot establish corruption.
The statutory presumption under Section 20 of the Act can only be drawn after the foundational fact of demand and voluntary acceptance is established by evidence.
If the complainant's testimony regarding demand is not supported by the shadow witness or independent corroboration, conviction cannot follow.
The prosecution cannot substitute suspicion or recovery for direct proof of the corrupt demand.
The trial court's assessment was a plausible view founded on the evidence, warranting no appellate interference with the acquittal.
Reaffirmed the cardinal principle that corruption charges must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

provisions.title: Sections 7, 13(1)(d), 20
provisions.relevance: Authoritative reiteration that proof of demand is the essential prerequisite to trigger statutory presumption and guilt.

provisions.title: Appeal against acquittal
provisions.relevance: Applied to protect trial court acquittal in bribery trap trials.

238.overview: The appellant was convicted under Section 21 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 for possessing commercial quantities of contraband. The appellant challenged the conviction before the Punjab & Haryana High Court on the ground that the search was conducted without complying with mandatory procedural safeguards under Section 50 of the Act.
238.issues: Whether compliance with Section 50 of the NDPS Act (informing the suspect of the right to be searched before a Gazetted Officer or Magistrate) is mandatory during personal search, and what is the effect of non-compliance on trial.
238.holding: The Punjab & Haryana High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted the appellant, holding that compliance with Section 50 of the NDPS Act during personal search is strictly mandatory. Failure to inform the suspect of their statutory option vitiates the recovery and trial.
key_findings: Section 50 of the NDPS Act provides a vital constitutional and statutory safeguard against false implication and planted recoveries.
The investigating officer has a mandatory duty to inform the suspect in clear terms of their legal right to be searched in the presence of a Gazetted Officer or Magistrate.
A third option offered by the police (e.g. 'or by the investigating officer himself') is contrary to the statutory mandate and vitiates the search.
Informing the suspect of their right under Section 50 must be proved by contemporaneous written communication signed by the suspect.
Non-compliance with Section 50 invalidates the search, rendering the recovered narcotics inadmissible in evidence.
Severe punishments prescribed under the NDPS Act require strict and meticulous adherence to procedural safeguards.
The trial court erred in convicting the accused despite admitted non-compliance with the mandatory statutory search procedure.

provisions.title: Conditions under which search of persons shall be conducted
provisions.relevance: Held to be strictly mandatory; failure to provide the option to be searched before a magistrate vitiates conviction.

provisions.title: Fair criminal procedure
provisions.relevance: Enforced to mandate strict compliance with statutory procedural safeguards in severe penal enactments.

239.overview: The Bihar Government issued an executive notification under Section 19(4) of the Bihar Excise Act, 1915 completely banning the manufacture, trade, possession, and consumption of Indian Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) throughout the State of Bihar. Liquor manufacturers, hoteliers, and distributors challenged the blanket prohibition as unconstitutional, arbitrary, and unreasonable.
239.issues: Whether the state's blanket notification banning all liquor trade and consumption violates Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 21 of the Constitution, and whether it was ultra vires the Bihar Excise Act, 1915.
239.holding: A Division Bench of the Patna High Court (Chief Justice I.A. Ansari and Justice Navaniti Prasad Singh) struck down the prohibition notification as unconstitutional, arbitrary, and ultra vires. The Court held that draconian penal provisions, collective community fines, and complete criminalization were disproportionate.
key_findings: While the State has the power under Article 47 (Directive Principles) to enforce prohibition, any statutory or executive measure must conform to Part III fundamental rights.
The notification imposed draconian, disproportionate penalties, including collective village fines and arresting entire families if liquor was found in a home, violating Article 14.
A citizen's choice of food, drink, and personal lifestyle consumed in the privacy of their home is a facet of personal liberty and privacy protected under Article 21.
The notification was issued arbitrarily under executive powers without following the statutory rule-making procedure prescribed under the Bihar Excise Act, 1915.
The complete embargo on the trade and possession of IMFL without allowing a reasonable transition period violated commercial fairness.
Directive Principles under Article 47 cannot be implemented by trampling on fundamental rights under Part III.
The state subsequently enacted a new comprehensive statute (Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016) to replace the invalidated notification.

provisions.title: Section 19(4): Prohibition notification
provisions.relevance: Executive notification struck down as ultra vires and manifestly arbitrary.

provisions.title: Right to Privacy and Personal Liberty
provisions.relevance: Applied to protect personal dietary choice and domestic privacy from draconic police searches.

provisions.title: Duty of the State to raise nutrition and improve public health (Prohibition)
provisions.relevance: Held to be non-justiciable and incapable of overriding core fundamental rights.

240.overview: Advocate Nikhil Soni filed a PIL before the Rajasthan High Court challenging the ancient Jain religious practice of 'Santhara' (also known as 'Sallekhana'—the voluntary fasting unto death by pious Jains upon feeling the approach of death or renouncing worldly life). The petitioner contended that the practice constitutes suicide punishable under Section 309 IPC and abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC.
240.issues: Whether the practice of Santhara / Sallekhana is an Essential Religious Practice (ERP) of Jainism protected under Article 25 of the Constitution, or whether it constitutes suicide punishable under Indian penal law.
240.holding: A Division Bench of the Rajasthan High Court held that Santhara is not an essential religious practice of Jainism and declared the practice to be an offence punishable under Section 306 (abetment of suicide) and Section 309 (attempt to commit suicide) of the Indian Penal Code.
key_findings: To qualify for constitutional protection under Article 25, a religious practice must be demonstrated to be an essential and integral part of the religion from scriptural antiquity.
The High Court held that the Jain community failed to establish that Santhara was an essential, obligatory religious tenet without which Jainism would cease to exist.
The right to freedom of religion under Article 25 is subject to 'public order, morality and health' and the other provisions of Part III.
The right to life under Article 21 does not include the right to extinguish life; taking one's life through voluntary starvation constitutes suicide under Section 309 IPC.
Those who facilitate, celebrate, or abet the practice of Santhara commit the offence of abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC.
The High Court directed the State Government to stop the practice and treat cases of Santhara as attempted suicides.
The Supreme Court of India granted an immediate stay on the Rajasthan High Court judgment in August 2015, preserving the practice pending final constitutional adjudication.

provisions.title: Freedom of religion
provisions.relevance: Evaluated under the Essential Religious Practices doctrine regarding voluntary fasting unto death.

provisions.title: Abetment and attempt to commit suicide
provisions.relevance: Applied by the High Court to criminalize Santhara (later stayed by the Supreme Court).

241.overview: Sunita Gandharva, the married daughter of a deceased government employee in Madhya Pradesh, applied for compassionate appointment following her father's death in harness. Her application was rejected under the State Policy on Compassionate Appointment, 2014, which explicitly excluded married daughters while extending eligibility to married sons.
241.issues: Whether the exclusion of married daughters from compassionate appointment schemes while including married sons violates Articles 14, 15, and 16 of the Constitution.
241.holding: A Full Bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court held that the policy clause excluding married daughters from consideration for compassionate appointment is unconstitutional, discriminatory, and void. The Court directed that married daughters must be treated on par with married sons.
key_findings: The exclusion of a daughter from compassionate appointment solely on the ground of her marriage is hostile discrimination based purely on sex under Article 15 and 16(2).
Marriage does not sever the emotional, familial, or economic bond between a daughter and her parents; a married daughter can and often does maintain her dependent parents.
Differentiating between married sons (eligible for compassionate appointment) and married daughters (ineligible) is founded on outdated patriarchal stereotypes.
The fundamental right to equality of opportunity in public employment under Article 16(2) strictly forbids discrimination based on sex.
Compassionate appointment is an exception to open recruitment designed to provide immediate financial relief to bereaved families; the family's dependency, not the gender of the child, is the test.
The word 'unmarried' in the state policy was struck down to include married daughters within the zone of consideration.
The state was directed to process the applicant's compassionate appointment application on merits without gender discrimination.

provisions.title: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sex in public employment
provisions.relevance: Directly applied to invalidate gender-discriminatory compassionate appointment clauses.

provisions.title: Equality before law
provisions.relevance: Struck down arbitrary discrimination between married sons and married daughters.

242.overview: In the ongoing National Register of Citizens (NRC) update process in Assam, a Foreigners Tribunal declared Monowara Bewa an illegal foreigner after rejecting a Gaon Panchayat Secretary certificate submitted by her to establish her linkage to her father (an Indian citizen). The Gauhati High Court had held that Panchayat certificates were private documents with zero evidentiary value.
242.issues: Whether certificates issued by Gaon Panchayat Secretaries have evidentiary value as linkage documents for proving citizenship in Foreigners Tribunal and NRC verification proceedings.
242.holding: The Gauhati High Court judgment was reviewed by the Supreme Court, which held that Gaon Panchayat certificates are admissible as linkage documents for married rural women, provided the contents and family relationships are verified through proper examination of the issuing authority.
key_findings: Millions of rural women in Assam marry at an early age without birth certificates or educational records, relying on village Panchayat certificates as their sole proof of lineage.
A Gaon Panchayat Secretary certificate is not a proof of Indian citizenship by itself; it is only a linkage document establishing parental relationship.
To be admitted as evidence, the certificate must be proved by producing the issuing official in court to verify the authenticity of the records.
Rejecting Panchayat linkage certificates wholesale would render millions of genuine rural Indian women stateless and disenfranchised.
The certificate must be subjected to thorough verification against electoral rolls and legacy data by NRC authorities.
Tribunals and courts must observe natural justice and cannot summarily declare individuals as foreigners without examining available linkage evidence.
Set the definitive verification framework for married women in the Assam NRC update process.

provisions.title: Section 6A: Special provisions as to citizenship of persons covered by Assam Accord
provisions.relevance: Central statutory framework governing citizenship verification and NRC in Assam.

provisions.title: Relevancy of entry in public record made in performance of duty
provisions.relevance: Applied to evaluate the evidentiary admissibility of Gaon Panchayat records.

243.overview: Former CBI Joint Director V.V. Lakshmi Narayana and trade unions filed a writ petition before the Telangana High Court challenging the Central Government's decision to privatize and disinvest 100% of its equity in the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant (Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited - RINL) under the Strategic Disinvestment Policy.
243.issues: Whether the Union Government's executive policy decision on strategic disinvestment of a public sector undertaking (PSU) is subject to judicial review under Article 226, and whether it violates employees' rights under Article 21.
243.holding: The Telangana High Court dismissed the writ petition, holding that strategic disinvestment is an economic policy decision of the Union Government that cannot be interfered with in judicial review unless shown to be illegal, unconstitutional, or manifestly arbitrary.
key_findings: Economic, fiscal, and disinvestment policies of the government lie squarely within the executive domain of policymaking.
Courts exercising writ jurisdiction under Article 226 lack the institutional expertise and economic mandate to evaluate complex privatization decisions.
The scope of judicial review in economic policy matters is narrow; courts will not interfere merely because a different economic policy is preferred by trade unions.
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) had evaluated the financial health, accumulated losses, and operational viability of RINL before approving disinvestment.
Employees do not possess a vested fundamental right under Article 21 to perpetual state employment in a commercial public sector undertaking.
The government owes a duty to protect employee interests by incorporating fair voluntary retirement schemes (VRS) and employee safeguards in transaction agreements.
Reiterated the doctrine of judicial restraint in economic policy decisions established in BALCO Employees Union.

provisions.title: Writ jurisdiction of High Court
provisions.relevance: Held subject to the doctrine of judicial self-restraint in macro-economic policy matters.

provisions.title: Equality and non-arbitrariness
provisions.relevance: Evaluated; policy upheld as non-arbitrary and backed by Cabinet Committee approvals.

244.overview: Farmers in the Amaravati region of Andhra Pradesh voluntarily surrendered over 33,000 acres of fertile agricultural land under a Land Pooling Scheme pursuant to the Andhra Pradesh Capital Region Development Authority (APCRDA) Act, 2014, in exchange for developed commercial plots in the unified capital city of Amaravati. In 2020, a new state government enacted laws to establish three separate capitals (Visakhapatnam, Kurnool, Amaravati) and repeal the APCRDA Act. Thousands of farmers challenged the laws.
244.issues: Whether the State Legislature has the legislative competence to enact laws shifting or trifurcating the capital city contrary to statutory agreements under the Land Pooling Scheme, and whether the state is bound by the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel.
244.holding: A 3-judge Special Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court delivered a historic verdict upholding the farmers' rights. The High Court held that the State Legislature lacked legislative competence to alter the capital city, declared the trifurcation laws unconstitutional, and directed the State Government to complete the Amaravati capital city project within six months under the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel.
key_findings: The State Government is bound by the solemn statutory agreements and representations made to farmers under the Land Pooling Scheme under the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel.
Farmers surrendered their ancestral lands relying on the State's commitment to develop a singular capital city; the State cannot renege on its promises.
The State Legislature lacked legislative competence to enact laws bifurcating or trifurcating the capital city in violation of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014.
The repeal of the APCRDA Act was arbitrary, unreasonable, and violative of Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
The High Court issued a writ of continuing mandamus directing the State Government to complete all trunk infrastructure, roads, and developed plots in Amaravati within six months.
The State was prohibited from alienating, mortgaging, or creating third-party rights over land pooled from farmers for any purpose other than the capital city.
Established a monumental precedent protecting citizens' property and contractual rights against arbitrary political policy reversals.

provisions.title: Andhra Pradesh Capital Region Development Authority Act
provisions.relevance: Enforced under the doctrine of promissory estoppel; attempted repeal held unconstitutional.

provisions.title: Equality and non-arbitrariness
provisions.relevance: Applied against sudden executive and legislative reversals causing catastrophic injury to farmers.

provisions.title: Right to property
provisions.relevance: Vindicated by prohibiting the state from misappropriating land surrendered under land pooling covenants.

245.overview: Hundreds of contractual high school and primary school teachers in Odisha who had rendered continuous service for over a decade filed writ petitions before the Orissa High Court seeking regularization of service and parity of pay scales with regularly appointed government teachers under the principle of 'Equal Pay for Equal Work'.
245.issues: Whether contractual teachers performing identical teaching duties as regular teachers are entitled to the benefit of 'Equal Pay for Equal Work' under Articles 14 and 39(d), and whether long-standing contractual employment can be regularized.
245.holding: The Orissa High Court held that paying contractual teachers substantially lower wages than regular teachers for performing identical duties violates Article 14 and the constitutional principle of 'Equal Pay for Equal Work'. The Court directed the State of Odisha to regularize the teachers and grant equal pay scales.
key_findings: The principle of 'Equal Pay for Equal Work' is an integral facet of Article 14 equality and Directive Principles under Article 39(d).
The State as a model employer cannot exploit educated youth by keeping them on contractual stipends for decades while extracting full-time pedagogical duties.
Contractual teachers possessed the requisite NCTE qualifications and taught the same curriculum and students as permanent cadre teachers.
Denying equal pay scales to teachers performing identical duties constitutes artificial, hostile discrimination under Article 14 and 16.
Quality education under Article 21A cannot be achieved by demotivating teachers through exploitative employment practices.
The State of Odisha was directed to formulate a comprehensive scheme to regularize contractual teachers who had completed satisfactory continuous service.
Directed the payment of minimum of the pay scale to all contractual teachers pending formal regularization.

provisions.title: Equality in public employment - Equal pay for equal work
provisions.relevance: Enforced to mandate pay parity and service regularization for contractual school teachers.

provisions.title: Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
provisions.relevance: Integrated into Article 14 as a substantive enforceable standard in state service jurisprudence.

provisions.title: Right to education
provisions.relevance: Harmonized to require fair service conditions for educators guaranteeing quality public education.
